evidence.disease: Large B-cell Lymphoma With IRF4 Rearrangement
evidence.evidence_statement: In this 2020 study the authors included twenty cases classified as IRF4 positive Large B-cell lymphomas (LBCL-IRF4). The patients were aged from 5 to 22 years (median of 14 years). All cases showed positivity by immunohistochemistry for MUM1 (protein encoded by IRF4) and BCL6. The rearrangement of IRF4 was confirmed by FISH for 17 cases and IGH involvement was detected in 7 cases. Through a targeted genome sequencing approach IRF4 and NF-κB-related genes (CARD11, CD79B, and MYD88) were found to be the most frequently mutated in LBCL-IRF4 cases. Copy number analysis by single-nucleotide polymorphism array platforms detected that LBCL-IRF4 cases had frequent 17p deletions and gains of chromosome 7 and 11q. Using a nanostring assay an overexpression of the downstream target genes of the NF-κB pathway were detected. The authors conclude that LBCL-IRF4 tumors have a distinct molecular profile.

JAK2 rerrangements were found to be one of genetic aberrations demonstrated in 15 cases of Ph-like ALL that were characterised using transcriptome and whole genome sequencing. As these are genetic alterations activating kinase or cytokine receptor signalling, these lesions could be sensitive to tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs). This paper documented the following JAK2 fusions: BCR::JAK2, STRN3::JAK2 and PAX5::JAK2. All JAK2 fusions identified in the study are in-frame and disrupt the pseudokinase domain of JAK2, which is thought to relieve autoinhibition of the kinase domain, resulting in a constitutively active fusion protein. The authors performed targeted analysis for these specific detected fusions in another 231 cases of high risk B-progenitor ALL from the COG AALL0232. They did not identify any othe cases with the same JAK2 fusions, however this does not rule out JAK2 fusions with other not targeted partners. JAK2 rearrangements were not identified in the MPN, CMML, and AML cohorts, and have not been detected in other childhood B-ALL subtypes studied by WGS and mRNA-seq, indicating they are highly enriched in Ph-like ALL. Flow cytometric phosphosignaling analysis on the cases with BCR::JAK2 and STRN3::JAK2 fusions demonstrated activation of downstream signaling pathways and tyrosine phosphorylation. This basal level of phosphorylation was then reduced with the JAK2 inhibitor XL019. Dasatinib was able to slightly inhibit tyrosine phosphorylation in the JAK2 cases. A BCR::JAK2 rearranged xenograft model was also tested to investigate the therapeutic efficacy of the JAK2 inhibitor ruxolitinib. There was a striking decrease in leukemic burden after 4 weeks of ruxolitinib treatment compared to vehicle-treated controls confirming the role of the BCR::JAK2 fusion as the key abnormality driving survival and proliferation of leukemia cells.

The authors describe the creation of a data portal containing over 20,000 gene fusions identified in 9,966 cancer samples and 648 normal samples from The Cancer Genome Atlas. The VPS18-NTRK3 e4::e18 fusion was detected in the colorectal tumor of a 71-year-old man (TCGA-A6-2674-01A).

Using a panel of three androgen-insensitive prostate cancer cell lines (C-81, CWR-R1 and 22Rv1), a novel AR protein isoform was identified. This protein was found to be encoded by three novel alternative splice AR isoforms. The isoforms were labeled AR3, AR4 and AR5. The AR3 isoform (commonly known as AR-V7) was found to be overexpressed in the androgen-insensitive prostate cancer cell lines used. Immunohistochemical cytoplasmic expression of AR3 was increased in androgen-insensitive prostate cancer cell lines as compared to their androgen-sensitive counterparts. Nuclear translocation of AR3 immunohistochemical staining was also noted in androgen-insensitive prostate cancer cell lines. Additionally, overexpression of AR3 in an androgen-sensitive prostate cancer cell line promoted tumour growth in androgen-depleted medium, while knockdown of AR3 expresssion in androgen-insensitive prostate cancer cell lines attenuated tumour growth in androgen-depleted medium.

Seven novel AR isoforms were identified through the examination of cryptic exon splicing at exon 3 of the AR gene. All seven isoforms encode truncated AR proteins, lacking the ligand binding domain. Two of these isoforms (AR-V1 and AR-V7) demonstrated overexpression in hormone refractory prostate cancer, as opposed to hormone naive prostate cancer, with associated immunohistochemical overexpression. In hormone refractory prostate cancer cell lines, nuclear localisation of prototypical AR protein was observed on androgen exposure, however, nuclear localisation of AR-V7 protein occurred in the absence of androgen exposure. AR-V7 was transfected into an AR-negative prostate cancer cell line, and induced PSA reporter gene and androgen responsive gene expression in an androgen-independent fashion.

In this study, the authors investigated the association of the RBM15::MRTFA fusion with acute megakaryoblastic leukemia (AMKL, FAB-M7), particularly in non-Down syndrome infants and young children. AMKL is a rare and heterogeneous aggresive disease that progresses rapidly, having a median patient survival of only eight months.The analysis focused on five patients, all infants and young children, diagnosed with AMKL carrying the t(1;22) translocation. Using fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH)-based positional cloning, the study defined the genomic breakpoints associated with the t(1;22) translocation. The researchers mapped breakpoints to a 28-kb intron on chromosome 22q13 and a 6-kb interval on chromosome 1p13. Subsequent analyses revealed a novel fusion gene, RBM15::MRTFA, resulting from the translocation. The RBM15::MRTFA fusion transcript encodes a chimeric protein that incorporates functional motifs from both genes, including RNA-recognition motifs (RRMs) from RBM15 and the SAP domain from MRTFA, potentially driving leukemogenesis through deregulation of RNA processing and altered transcriptional activity. This study highlights the central pathogenic role of the RBM15::MRTFA fusion in AMKL and its diagnostic significance, drawing parallels with other fusion-driven leukemias such as PML::RARA in acute promyelocytic leukemia. The findings emphasize the value of molecular diagnostics in identifying rare but critical genetic markers, underscoring the RBM15::MRTFA fusion as a key diagnostic and potentially therapeutic target in AMKL.

In this study, the authors explored the genomic landscape of acute megakaryoblastic leukemia (AMKL) in patients without Down syndrome (non-DS-AMKL). AMKL is a rare and heterogeneous subtype of acute myeloid leukemia (AML) with poor outcomes. The analysis included 99 patients, comprising 75 pediatric cases (infants and children) and 24 adult cases, making it the largest cohort of non-DS-AMKL to undergo next-generation sequencing to date. Using RNA and exome sequencing, the study identified seven genomic subgroups in pediatric non-DS-AMKL, characterized by distinct chimeric oncogenes and cooperating mutations. Among these, the RBM15::MRTFA (also known as RBM15-MKL1) fusion was detected in 10.5% of pediatric cases. This fusion, resulting from the recurrent t(1;22) translocation, was predominantly observed in infants. The RBM15::MRTFA fusion encodes a chimeric protein that integrates functional motifs from both genes, leading to aberrant regulation of RNA processing, transcriptional activity, and megakaryoblast proliferation. The study emphasized the the clinical importance of stratifying non-DS-AMKL patients by genomic subtypes and underscored RBM15::MRTFA fusion and a defining oncogenic driver for one of the molecular subtypes of AMKL.

In this study, the authors performed an international retrospective analysis of 490 pediatric patients (≤18 years) with non–Down syndrome acute megakaryoblastic leukemia (non-DS-AMKL), a rare and aggressive subtype of acute myeloid leukemia (AML), diagnosed between 1989 and 2009. The cohort, with a median age of 1.53 years, represents one of the largest studies to date on this leukemia subtype. Cytogenetic analysis, available for 372 patients (75.9%), identified the t(1;22)(p13;q13) translocation, associated with the RBM15::MRTFA (RBM15-MKL1) fusion, in 13.7% of cases. This translocation was predominantly observed in infants, with a median age of 0.55 years, and was more common in females (64.7%). The RBM15::MRTFA fusion gene, restricted to AMKL, encodes a chimeric protein that disrupts normal transcriptional regulation, aiding in leukemogenesis. The study highlighted the diagnostic significance of identifying t(1;22) through cytogenetic and molecular methods, such as fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) and reverse-transcriptase polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR). The findings underscore the critical role of the RBM15::MRTFA fusion as a diagnostic marker for a subtype of non-DS-AMKL.

In this phase 3 trial, patients with chemorefractory metastatic colorectal cancer harbouring KRAS G12C mutations were assigned to one of three groups. The first group received 960 mg of sotorasib (KRAS G12C inhibitor) once daily plus panitumumab (n = 53), the second group received 240 mg of sotorasib once daily plus panitumumab (n=53), and the third group received investigator's choice of trifluridine-tipiracil or regorafenib/standard-care (n=54). The median PFS was 5.6 months (95% CI, 4.2-6.3) in the 960-mg sotorasib-panitumumab, 3.9 months (95% CI, 3.6-5.7) in the 240-mg sotorasib-panitumumab, and 2.0 months (95% CI, 1.9-3.9) in the standard care group. The hazard ratio for disease progression or death compared to the standard care cohort was 0.48 (95% CI, 0.30-0.78, p=0.005) in the 960-mg sotorasib-panitumumab group and 0.59 (95% CI, 0.37-0.95, p=0.036) in the 240-mg sotorasib-panitumumab group. The ORR was 26.4% (95% CI, 15.3 to 40.3), 5.7% (95% CI, 1.2 to 15.7), and 0% (95% CI, 0.0 to 6.6) in the 960-mg sotorasib–panitumumab, 240-mg sotorasib–panitumumab, and standard-care groups, respectively. Grade 3 or higher treatment-related adverse effects occurred in 35.8% of the 960-mg sotorasib-panitumumab group, 30.2% of the 240-mg sotorasib-panitumumab group, and 43.1% in the standard care group. Overall, the study concluded that the 960-mg sotorasib-panitumumab group resulted in a longer PFS compared to the standard treatment, and toxic effects were expected with limited discontinuation.

profile.name: KRAS G12C
profile.summary: While the KRAS G12 region is a widely studied recurrent region in cancer, its impact on clinical action is still debated. Often associated with tumors that are wild-type for other drivers (EGFR and ALK specifically), the prognosis for patients with this mutation seems to be worse than the KRAS wild-type cohort in patients with colorectal and pancreatic cancer, however this hypothesis is in need of further validation. This mutation, along with the mutations affecting the neighboring G13 position, may result in a less responsive tumor when treated with first-generation TKI's like gefitinib. However, cetuximab treatment was shown to extend survival in a cohort of colorectal patients.

evidence.evidence_statement: In this study, the authors characterized 77 pediatric Ph-like B-ALL cases from the Dutch Childhood Oncology Group trials and German Cooperative ALL trials, and identified 5 cases with activated JAK signaling pathway. Specifically, there were three cases of PAX5::JAK2, one each of BCR::JAK2 and TERF2::JAK2. As the TERF2::JAK2 fusion was novel, it was additionally characterized. The fusion breakpoint was found to occur in TERF2 exon 10-JAK2 exon 19 with a deletion of the last 11 coding nucleotides of TERF2 exon 10. Overall, the authors found that JAK2 fusions comprised 6.5% of their Ph-like ALL cohort (n=77). In terms of clinical response to induction therapy, two out of five of the cases with JAK2 fusions (BCR::JAK2 and TERF2::JAK2) resulted in relapsed disease.

In this study, researchers examined the diagnostic significance of the PML::RARA fusion in acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL, FAB-M3), a subtype of acute myeloid leukemia (AML) associated with the t(15;17)(q24.1;q21.2) translocation. This chromosomal rearrangement leads to the formation of the PML::RARA fusion gene, which disrupts myeloid differentiation and results in the accumulation of abnormal promyelocytes in the bone marrow. The study focused on a pediatric female patient with APL who uniquely exhibited all three known PML::RARA transcript variants (bcr1, bcr2, and bcr3) simultaneously—an extremely rare occurrence not previously documented. These transcript variants were identified using multiple molecular techniques, including reverse transcription-quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR), HemaVision-28N Multiplex RT-qPCR, HemaVision-28Q qualitative RT-qPCR, and the AmpliSeq RNA Myeloid Panel. Further molecular analysis, including gene expression profiling via microarray, revealed upregulation of genes such as CCL1 and α- and β-defensins—markers rarely observed in AML but with potential diagnostic relevance in APL. These findings underscore the pivotal role of PML::RARA fusion in APL diagnosis and highlight the importance of molecular diagnostics in enhancing diagnostic accuracy and prognostic assessment.

profile.name: PML::RARA Fusion
profile.summary: The PML-RARA fusion is seen as a diagnostic event in acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL). Both in vitro and in vivo studies have shown sensitivity to ATRA in APL patients harboring the PML-RARa fusion. Recent interest has been shown in combining ATRA and arsenic trioxide for treating these patients, and early results seem promising.

evidence.evidence_statement: This study presents a rare case of acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) characterized by an atypical PML::RARA fusion transcript resulting from the t(15;17) translocation. The patient, a 44-year-old female, was diagnosed through morphological, cytogenetic, and molecular analyses, including fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH), which confirmed the presence of t(15;17). RT-PCR revealed bands of unusual sizes, distinct from the typical PML::RARA breakpoints (bcr1, bcr2, bcr3). Sequencing identified a rare bcr2 transcript with a breakpoint in PML exon 6, which is still expected to produce a functional chimeric protein. This case reinforces the diagnostic significance of PML::RARA fusion in APL.

Recent interest has been shown in combining ATRA and arsenic trioxide for treating these patients, and early results seem promising.

evidence.evidence_statement: In this study, the authors investigated the molecular characteristics of acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) in patients with atypical PML::RARA fusion transcripts. APL is a rare and aggressive leukemia subtype characterized by the t(15;17) translocation, which generates the PML::RARA fusion gene. The study focused on three adult patients diagnosed with APL, all carrying novel atypical PML::RARA fusion transcripts that were undetectable using standard molecular assays. Using reverse transcriptase polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) and direct sequencing, the researchers identified abnormal-sized PCR products in these patients, indicating the presence of atypical fusion transcripts. Additional molecular analysis, including patient-specific quantitative real-time PCR (Q-RT-PCR), was conducted to monitor minimal residual disease (MRD) and evaluate therapeutic response. The study found a range of PCR product sizes, including 180 bp, 649 bp, and 505 bp in one patient, with other variations observed in the remaining two cases. This research highlights the clinical and biological significance of atypical PML::RARA fusion transcripts in APL, emphasizing their potential impact on diagnosis and treatment. The findings demonstrate that these atypical isoforms can complicate molecular detection, posing challenges for standard diagnostic assays. However, the study reaffirms that APL diagnosis is always associated with the presence of a PML::RARA fusion transcript, which in some cases requires specialized techniques for accurate identification.

evidence.evidence_statement: In this study, the authors investigated the role of the ETV6::RUNX1 fusion in the diagnosis of B-lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma. B-ALL is a heterogeneous disease, and identifying cytogenetic abnormalities allows accurate stratification into genetically defined subtypes. The analysis included 342 children diagnosed with B-ALL, among whom 99 cases (28.9%) were positive for the ETV6::RUNX1 fusion, detected using polymerase chain reaction (PCR)-based molecular screening. The translocation t(12;21)(p13;q22) results in the fusion of ETV6 (TEL) on chromosome 12 and RUNX1 (AML1) on chromosome 21, creating a chimeric protein that disrupts normal hematopoietic differentiation and contributes to leukemogenesis. The study findings indicate that patients with the ETV6::RUNX1 fusion have a better event-free survival (EFS) compared to those without the fusion. While only 3% of ETV6::RUNX1-positive patients relapsed, the relapse rate in ETV6::RUNX1-negative cases was significantly higher (11.1%). This study underscores the diagnostic significance of the ETV6::RUNX1 fusion, highlighting its role as a key molecular marker in pediatric B-ALL.

evidence.disease: Acute Myeloid Leukaemia With FUS::ERG Fusion
evidence.evidence_statement: This study investigates the diagnostic importance of the translocation t(16;21)(p11;q22), resulting in the TLS/FUS::ERG fusion gene, in acute myeloid leukemia (AML). The authors utilized RT-PCR to detect the TLS/FUS::ERG chimeric transcripts in 19 AML cases with the t(16;21)(p11;q22) identified through karyotype analysis. The median age at diagnosis was 22 years (range 2 to 61 years ). The fusion transcript was consistently detected, even during remission, suggesting its role in identifying persistent leukemic cells and potential chemoresistance. The reliable detection of the TLS/FUS::ERG chimeric transcripts at diagnosis demonstrates their utility as a highly sensitive molecular marker for initial AML diagnosis and ongoing disease monitoring. The study also identified a novel transcript variant (Type D), characterized by an additional 138 nucleotides from TLS/FUS exon 8 and ERG exons 7 and 8, which highlights increased molecular heterogeneity in this genetic alteration. This research emphasizes the diagnostic relevance of the t(16;21) translocation across various French-American-British (FAB) subtypes of AML, providing valuable insight for improved diagnostic accuracy in AML patients.

evidence.disease: Acute Myeloid Leukaemia With FUS::ERG Fusion
evidence.evidence_statement: This international retrospective study investigates the diagnostic features of acute myeloid leukemia (AML) with the t(16;21) translocation resulting in the FUS::ERG fusion gene in pediatric patients. Data were gathered from 14 cohorts within the Berlin-Frankfurt-Münster (I-BFM) Study Group, encompassing 31 cases exhibiting the FUS::ERG with a median age of 9 years (range 2 to 18 years). AML with t(16;21) did not show a predominance in any specific FAB classification and was frequently associated with complex karyotypes, including trisomy 8 and trisomy 10. Notably, FUS::ERG AML often presented with eosinophilia, micromegakaryocytes, and hemophagocytosis. Standard karyotyping may fail to detect the translocation, necessitating the use of more sensitive diagnostic methods such as FISH, RT-PCR, or RNA sequencing. Although 87% of patients achieved remission, 74% experienced relapse, most within the first year, and minimal residual disease (MRD) negativity did not predict relapse-free survival, indicating the presence of chemoresistant leukemic stem cells. Gene expression profiling revealed a distinct molecular signature, with altered retinoic acid signaling, which may offer potential therapeutic targets. The study highlights the unique diagnostic characteristics of AML with t(16;21), reinforcing the need for specialized molecular testing and offering insight into its distinct biological and clinical features.

evidence.evidence_statement: This study focuses on the diagnostic characteristics of pediatric patients with the t(16;21)(p11;q22)/FUS::ERG translocation using advanced molecular methods. The authors studied four cases of pediatric AML with a median age of 3 years (range 2 to 5 years) in which karyotype analysis revealed the t(16;21)(p11;q22) resultig in the FUS::ERG fusion. They identified multiple FUS::ERG transcript variants, including a novel fusion where FUS exon 7 fuses with ERG exon 9, complicating minimal residual disease (MRD) detection. To improve diagnostic accuracy, next-generation sequencing and long-range PCR were used to precisely map breakpoints at the DNA level. Cytogenetic analysis revealed the t(16;21) translocation either as an isolated abnormality or in combination with trisomy 8 and del(9), accompanied by distinct immunophenotypic features such as high CD56 expression. Additionally, mutations in DNMT3A, ASXL1, BCOR, and RUNX1 were detected, suggesting clonal evolution prior to FUS::ERG transformation. These molecular findings highlight the complexity of diagnosing this specific AML subtype, underscoring the importance of utilizing sensitive techniques such as next-generation sequencing and long-range PCR for accurate detection of FUS::ERG and related genetic alterations.

This study investigated the role of TFCP2-related gene fusions in primary intraosseous rhabdomyosarcomas (PIOS), particularly within spindle cell and sclerosing rhabdomyosarcoma subtypes. The analysis included seven patients with tumors located in the iliac bone, femur, maxilla, and skull, all exhibiting spindle cell morphology. Among the five cases tested for TFCP2-related gene abnormalities, three harbored an EWSR1::TFCP2 fusion, one had a FUS::TFCP2 fusion, and another showed a FUS rearrangement without TFCP2 involvement. Morphologically, TFCP2 fusion-associated tumors were composed of spindle cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm, arranged in short fascicles or sheets, with some cases also displaying epithelioid cells. Immunohistochemically, these tumors were diffusely positive for desmin, focally positive for myogenin, cytokeratin, and ALK. These findings highlight the diagnostic significance of TFCP2-related fusions in spindle cell and sclerosing rhabdomyosarcomas, distinguishing them as a rare subtype of bone rhabdomyosarcoma.

This 2018 study highlighted the diagnostic role of the FUS::TFCP2 fusion in spindle cell/sclerosing rhabdomyosarcoma (sRMS) through a single-case study of a primary spindle cell rhabdomyosarcoma of bone. The tumor harbored an in-frame fusion joining exon 6 of FUS to exon 2 of TFCP2, resembling previously reported cases of aggressive rhabdomyosarcoma. The fusion was confirmed using FISH, RT-PCR, and Sanger sequencing, establishing it as a key molecular feature. RNA-sequencing analysis demonstrated overexpression of ALK, TERT, MYOD1, and multiple keratin genes, distinguishing the tumor from normal skeletal muscle. Chromosomal microarray revealed a tetraploid complement, an unbalanced 16p11.2 rearrangement disrupting FUS, and CDKN2A deletion, suggesting genomic instability. Histologically, the tumor showed monomorphic spindle cell morphology, strong MyoD1 and desmin expression, limited myogenin expression, and ALK positivity. These findings underscore the diagnostic value of the FUS::TFCP2 fusion in identifying a genetically distinct and aggressive subset of sRMS, reinforcing its role as a molecular marker.

This is the first case report of cribriform neuroepithelial tumor (CRINET), a rare brain cancer identified in a 26-month-old girl and a 10-month-old boy, affecting the third and fourth ventricles. Histologically, CRINET is a non-rhabdoid neoplasm with cribriform strands and a trabecular pattern, distinct from atypical teratoid/rhabdoid tumors (AT/RT). Immunohistochemistry revealed a loss of nuclear INI1 (encoded by SMARCB1) expression in tumor cells, while surrounding vascular cells and infiltrating lymphocytes demonstrated a normal pattern of retained staining. Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) detected no structural alterations at the SMARCB1 locus in 22q11.2. However, sequencing of SMARCB1 identified a homozygous 4-bp duplication within exon 4 (492dupCCTT), causing a premature stop codon in one case, with no mutations found in the other. In conclusion, CRINET is a non-rhabdoid intraventricular and periventricular intracranial tumor characterized by loss of INI1 expression.

evidence.evidence_statement: This study explored the molecular features of cribriform neuroepithelial tumors (CRINET) using multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplification (MLPA) and molecular inversion profiling (MIP) assays alongside targeted sequencing. The analysis included 3 cases that exhibited the characteristic CRINET feature of INI1 protein loss (encoded by SMARCB1 on 22q11.2). MLPA and SMARCB1 sequencing identified an allelic loss on 22q with an exon 4 CCTT duplication (492dupCCTT) in case 1 and a p.T381R mutation in case 3. A homozygous deletion of exons 7 and 8 of SMARCB1 was found in case 2. MIP analysis revealed a stable genomic profile, with no large chromosomal changes beyond 22q loss, though copy number gains were detected in several cancer genes in individual cases. Collectively, this study confirmed previous findings that identify SMARCB1 as the key gene in CRINET pathogenesis.

profile.name: SMARCB1 LOSS OF NUCLEAR PROTEIN EXPRESSION

evidence.evidence_statement: This study compared cribriform neuroepithelial tumor (CRINET) and atypical teratoid/rhabdoid tumor (AT/RT) to determine whether CRINET is a distinct entity or a variant of AT/RT. The study contained 10 CRINET samples, including 6 previously reported cases, and 30 AT/RT samples, with 10 samples from each of the three AT/RT subgroups (ATRT-TYR, ATRT-SHH, and ATRT-MYC). Molecular profiling used Infinium HumanMethylation450 arrays, SMARCB1 fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH), multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplification (MLPA), and sequencing. Additionally, the survival outcome of the CRINET cohort was compared to a larger cohort of 27 patients with ATRT-TYR. Anatomical sites of CRINETs included supratentorial, infratentorial and lateral ventricle locations. CRINET cases showed diverse SMARCB1 alterations in copy number and mutations. 9 of 10 cases of CRINET harboured large heterozygous chr22q deletions inclusive of the SMARCB1 gene, with SMARCB1 mutations in the other allele in 5 cases (2 of which were germline). Methylation profiling placed CRINET within the AT/RT-tyrosinase (TYR) subgroup. Histologically, CRINET exhibited distinct morphology from AT/RT-TYR, although all CRINET cases and 9/10 AT/RT-TYR cases showed immunohistochemical staining for tyrosinase. Clinically, CRINET patients (n=10) showed better survival than ATRT-TYR patients (n=27). Mean overall survival was 125 months (95% CI: 100–151) for CRINET and 53 months (95% CI: 33–74) for ATRT-TYR. This study highlights key histopathologic and prognostic differences between CRINET and AT/RT-TYR. The results show that CRINET should be considered a separate entity although SMARCB1 abnormalities play the key role in pathogenesis of both AT/RT and CRINET.

evidence.evidence_statement: In this study, the authors explored the role of retinoic acid receptor alpha (RARα) gene rearrangements in acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) and their connection to the t(15;17) chromosomal translocation. Using molecular and cytogenetic analyses, they examined eight APL patients and the NB4 cell line, derived from an APL patient. The study identified a RARα fusion transcript, formed by the translocation of RARα from chromosome 17 to the partner gene on chromosome 15. Southern blot analysis detected RARα gene rearrangements in six of the eight APL patients, while these alterations were absent in normal and non-APL leukemic controls. These findings strongly implicate RARα in APL leukemogenesis and suggest that the t(15;17) translocation results in a fusion gene that disrupts normal RARα function, contributing to the disease. The study further highlights the importance of molecular testing for RARα rearrangements as a diagnostic marker for APL.

evidence.evidence_statement: In this study, the authors investigated the role of retinoic acid receptor alpha (RARα) gene rearrangements in acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL), a distinct subtype of acute myeloid leukemia (AML) characterized by the t(15;17) chromosomal translocation. The study analyzed 20 APL cases, of which 18 exhibited the t(15;17) translocation, while 2 had a normal karyotype. Using Southern and Northern blot analyses, the authors identified RARα gene rearrangements and aberrant transcripts exclusively in APL cases, but not in other neoplastic conditions or normal controls. These findings suggest that RARα is directly involved in the APL chromosome 17 breakpoint and plays a crucial role in leukemogenesis. The study highlights the diagnostic significance of RARα gene alterations, as their presence can serve as a molecular marker for identifying leukemic promyelocytes in APL.

evidence.evidence_statement: In this study, the authors investigated the diagnostic role of TFCP2 fusions in spindle cell/sclerosing rhabdomyosarcoma (SC/S-RMS), a rare and aggressive subtype of rhabdomyosarcoma. While SC/S-RMS encompasses molecularly distinct subgroups, recent RNA sequencing studies have identified a novel subset defined by TFCP2 rearrangements. The analysis focused on 14 cases, highlighting their unique clinicopathological and molecular characteristics. Using fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH), array-comparative genomic hybridization (array-CGH), RNA sequencing, and targeted next-generation sequencing, the study confirmed the presence of TFCP2 fusions with either EWSR1 (n=6) or FUS (n=8). These tumors predominantly arose in bone (12/14), with a striking predilection for the craniofacial skeleton, an unusual site for rhabdomyosarcoma. Morphologically, they displayed a spindle cell and epithelioid pattern, frequently expressing myogenic markers (MYF4 and/or MYOD1) and keratins. ALK over-expression was observed in most cases, often associated with internal deletions rather than gene fusions. Genomic profiling revealed complex rearrangements, including recurrent CDKN2A deletions and high genomic instability. This study establishes TFCP2 fusions as a defining feature of a distinct spindle cell/sclerosing rhabdomyosarcoma subtype. The findings underscore the diagnostic utility of TFCP2 rearrangement testing in distinguishing this entity from other rhabdomyosarcoma subtypes and suggest ALK over-expression as a potential therapeutic target.

In this 2022 study the authors included 4 cases of sinonasal acinic cell carcinoma and 10 acinic cell carcinoma cases of the parotid gland. All four sinonasal patients were male, aged from 27 to 70 years. Using immunohistochemistry they detected positive NR4A3 nuclear staining in all 14 cases, while negative nuclear staining was observed in 39 other sinonasal tumors. In 3 of the 4 sinonasal Acinic cell carcinoma evaluated by NR4A3 break apart FISH, they tested positive to a rearrangement. Using RT-PCR the authors detected a significant increase in NR4A3 mRNA levels in all salivary gland and sinonasal acinic cell carcinoma patients compared with normal parotid gland tissue. The authors conclude that this is the first study to show that NR4A3 could serve as a reliable marker to distinguish sinonasal acinic cell carcinoma from other sinonasal tumors.

In this 2023 study the authors included 4 cases of acinic cell carcinoma of the salivary gland. The age of the patients ranged from 13 to 16 years, and included 2 males and 2 females. Immunohistochemistry showed the tumour cells from all four patients had strong, diffuse nuclear positive staining to NR4A3, while the adjacent benign salivary tissue was negative. In this study the authors considered NR4A3 immunohistochemical staining as a surrogate marker for t(4;9)(q13;q31) and a highly sensitive and specific marker for acinic cell carcinoma.

A 48 year old male with lung adenocarcinoma who was a smoker presented with diminished vision and tinnitus, and multiple intracranial brain metastasis were identified by CT. Metastatic site was submitted for molecular profiling. Histopathological analysis confirmed diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, and immunophenotyping confirmed this. ALK protein expression was negative. NGS identified EGFR::RAD51 fusion at the metastatic site, and reduction in copy number of CDKN2A. Breakpoints were intron 24 for EGFR (NM_005228 chr7:55,268,165) and intron 3 of RAD51 (NM_002875 chr15:40,994,701) using hg19. Erlotinib 150 mg/qd was administered and decrease in tumor size was seen after one month via CT scan, and this was classified as partial response, with stable disease after 5 months treatment. The authors conclude that this case report supports erlotinib treatment of EGFR::RAD51 fusion NSCLC patients.

A 62 year-old female never smoker diagnosed of lung adenocarcinoma that was negative for EGFR and ALK alterations (EGFR hotspot tissue NGS) was treated with carboplatin/ pemetrexed/ bevacizumab (x 6 cycles) followed by maintenance (x4 cycles) prior to PD. She then went on nivolumab (x6 cycles) until Progressive Disease (PD) with pleural effusion and brain metastasis. An EGFR::RAD51 fusion was detected in the pleural fluid by Foundation Medicine. The DNA fusion consists of EGFR exons 1-24 (breakpoint in EGFR intron 24) coupled to RAD51 exons 4-10 (breakpoint in RAD51 intron 3). Patient was treated with afatinib (at 40 mg/d, then 30 mg/d) following detection of the EGFR::RAD51 fusion and showed stable disease after 6 months. The authors note that EGFR::RAD51 was not seen in earlier assays of the tumor, and state that this might be due to the appearance of the fusion during tumor evolution, or due to it being missed by earlier assays. They note that other detections of the fusion came from Foundation Medicine assays, and most other assays are not designed to cover EGFR exons 24 and 25.

This is a case report of 29-year-old diagnosed with metastatic adenocarcinoma of the left lung. The patient was treated with chemotherapy (cisplatin 75 mg/m2 and pemetrexed 500 mg/m2 every 3 weeks) and immunotherapy (pembrolizumab 200 mg every 3 weeks) for 4 cycles then maintenance with pembrolizumab and pemetrexed for 4 cycles before PD on lungs, brain and lymph nodes. FoundationOne DX1 on a new mediastinal lymph node biopsy detected an EGFR::RAD51 fusion. Patient was then treated with erlotinib (150mg/d) and achieved PR on all tumour sites three weeks following treatment initiation. The patient was switched to Osimertinib (80 mg/d) after being on erlotinib for two months due to renal toxicity. Further tumour response was observed at subsequent restating imaging and the patient is still on treatment 10 months since EGFR-TKI initiation.

This is a case report of a 45-year-old male never smoker that was diagnosed with metastatic lung adenocarcinoma. The patient responded poorly to the initial chemoimmunotherapy (carboplatin, pemetrexed, nivolumab, and ipilimumab) and progressively deteriorated. Following the detection of an EGFR::RAD51 gene fusion by repeat NGS using FoundationOne Liquid CDx, the patient was treated with Osimertinib (80mg/d) and experienced dramatic symptom improvement within one month of treatment initiation. Despite asymptomatic intracranial metastases with stable systemic disease at 9 months, the patient remained on therapy and continued to show PR 12 months after initiation of Osimertinib.

In this study, the authors characterized the TEL (currently ETV6)::AML1 (currently RUNX1) gene fusion in B-lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL) with the t(12;21)(p12;q22) using cytogenetic and molecular methods, including FISH, PCR, Southern blot hybridization, and sequencing. Analysis of nine patient specimens (two AML, seven B-ALL) and two cell lines revealed that the TEL (ETV6) gene breakpoint in t(12;21)(p12;q22) differs from the one in t(5;12)(q33;p13) seen in Chronic Myelomonocytic Leukemia (CMML). The TEL (ETV6) gene remained active on both derivative chromosomes, with der(21) expressing a 5’ ETV6::3'RUNX1 fusion transcript lacking the ETS DNA-binding domain, while der(12) expressed the ETS domain under an unknown promoter (G4). Additionally, ETV6 was deleted from the normal chromosome 12. The breakpoint in the RUNX1 gene was at its 5’ end, upstream of breakpoints in other myeloid malignancies [t(8;21), t(3;21)]. The ETV6::RUNX1 fusion protein retained helix-loop-helix (HLH) domain from the ETV6-encoded protein which interacts with transcriptional regulators, and nearly entire RUNX1-encoded protein. The chimeric protein was predicted to cause dysregulated transcription of lymphoid lineage-specific genes. These findings provide insight into the molecular mechanisms of ETV6::RUNX1-driven leukemogenesis in B-ALL.

In this study, the authors investigated the t(12;21)(p13;q22) in pediatric acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL). The t(12;21) is typically not visible by karyotype analysis and is rarely detected by conventional cytogenetics (<0.05% of cases). However, using molecular techniques, the authors identified the resulting TEL::AML1 (known currently as ETV6::RUNX1) fusion transcript in 22% of pediatric ALL patients, making it the most frequent genetic alteration in this disease. The TEL::AML1 (ETV6::RUNX1) fusion results from the rearrangement of TEL (ETV6), a helix-loop-helix ETS-like transcription factor, and AML1 (RUNX1), the DNA-binding subunit of the core-binding factor (CBF) transcription complex. Patients harboring the TEL::AML1 (ETV6::RUNX1) fusion exhibited distinct clinical features, including an age range of 1 to 10 years, B-lineage immunophenotype, non-hyperdiploid DNA content, and an excellent prognosis. These findings underscore the role of ETV6::RUNX1 fusion in defining a common and clinically relevant subtype of pediatric B-ALL.

evidence.evidence_statement: In this 2016 study the authors included 153 pediatric non-Down syndrome patients diagnosed with acute megakaryoblastic leukemia (AMKL) which is a rare subtype of acute myeloid leukemia. All patients were screened for NUP98::KDM5A, CBFA2T3::GLIS2, RBM15::MKL1 and KMT2A rearrangements with polymerase chain reaction (PCR). The PCR primers for NUP98::KDM5A were designed to detect a NUP98 exon 12 fusion to exon 27 of KDM5A. The NUP98::KDM5A gene fusion was detected in 14 patients (9%) with a median age of 1.9 years (range 0.8-8.5); it was mutually exclusive with other tested fusions and its' presence was associated with an unfavorable outcome. The NUP98::KDM5A fusion is the primary abnormality in a subtype of pediatric AML commonly presenting with magakaryoblastic differentiation and associated with a poor clinical outcome.

evidence.disease: Acute Myeloid Leukemia With NUP98 Rearrangement
evidence.evidence_statement: In this 2011 study the authors included pediatric and adult cohorts of patients diagnosed with acute myeloid leukemia (AML). Initially, using RT-PCR, they detected the cytogenetically cryptic NUP98::NSD1 in-frame gene fusion of NUP98 exon 12 to exon 6 of NSD1 in 2/45 pediatric cytogenetically normal AML (CN-AML) patients and in 1/47 adult CN-AML cases. A further 1101 AML cases were then screened using RT-PCR and the identical NUP98::NSD1 in-frame fusion was detected in 23 (2.1%) cases. The NUP98::NSD1 fusion was detected more frequently in pediatric patients with a median age of onset at 17 years (range 2 to 63), and was particularly frequent in children when considering only the CN-AML cases. Three additional cases with cytogenetically visible 11p15-aberrations were also confirmed to have NUP98 gene fusions, however with alternate partners including JARID1A, TOP1 and DDX10. NUP98::NSD1 was frequently associated with FLT3 ITD (91% of cases) and WT1 mutations (45% of cases). The authors conclude that the cryptic NUP98::NSD1 fusion defines a previously unrecognized group of young AML patients associated with an unfavorable outcome and routine screening for NUP98::NSD1 at diagnosis is essential.

evidence.evidence_statement: In this 2014 study the authors investigated the presence of NUP98::NSD1 fusion in pediatric and adult acute myeloid leukemia (AML) patients. Utilizing reverse transcriptase-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) the NUP98::NSD1 fusion was identified in 39/920 (4%) patients. Since 36 of the 39 NUP98::NSD1 patients were either FLT3 ITD positive or cytogenetically normal (CN-AML) a further 620 patients who harbored FLT3 ITD and/or CN-AML were included for screening, with the NUP98::NSD1 identified in 63 (10%) patients. All patients harbored the identical in-frame fusion of NUP98 exon 12 and NSD1 exon 6. Age of patients with NUP98::NSD1 varied from <1 to 50 years of age (median, 10 years), indicating that NUP98::NSD1 is more frequent in younger age. NUP98::NSD1 cases frequently (82%) harbored a FLT3 ITD, and 26% harbored simultaneously FLT3 ITD and WT1 mutations. The authors conclude that the NUP98::NSD1 fusion, frequently co-occurring with FLT3 ITD, defines a subgroup of AML patients at very high risk for induction failure; the study supports upfront screening of CN-AML for the cytogenetically cryptic NUP98::NSD1 fusion.

disease.label: Acute Myeloid Leukemia With NUP98 Rearrangement
Acute Myeloid Leukemia With NUP98 Rearrangement

evidence.disease: Acute Myeloid Leukemia With NUP98 Rearrangement
evidence.evidence_statement: In this 2023 study the authors included 2,235 children and young adults diagnosed with acute myeloid leukemia (AML). NUP98 fusions were detected in these patients either by karyotype of RNA sequencing. Overall 160 patients (7.2%) were identified to have a NUP98 rearrangement. The most common NUP98 translocations were NUP98::NSD1 (108/160) and NUP98::KDM5A (32/160), however 20 patients were detected with 13 different NUP98 translocation partners, including HOXA9 (n=4), HOXD13 (n=3), PHF15 (n=2), PHF23 (n=2) and single cases of BPTF, BRWD3, DDX10, HMGB3, HOXA13, KAT7, PRRX1, SET, and TOP1. NUP98 fusions were enriched in children aged 3-10 years old. NUP98 fusion breakpoints by RNA sequencing revealed a high diversity of NUP98 exon junctions, although 85% of NUP98 fusions had a breakpoint junction in exon 12 or 13, the remaining cases had breakpoints occurring in various positions from exon 11 to exon 29. The NUP98::KDM5A immunophenotype corresponded to megakaryocytic maturation. For NUP98:NSD1 cases, enrichment of FLT3 ITD (74%) and WT1 mutations (42%) was detected. The authors conclude that NUP98 fusions constitute a highly refractory class of AML, regardless of fusion partner.

In this 2018 study, the authors analyzed tumor samples from 13 patients diagnosed with IG-MYC–positive neoplasms exhibiting a precursor B-cell phenotype. This entity is molecularly distinct from classical Burkitt lymphoma (BL), which arises from mature germinal center B cells, whereas these cases originate from the same immature B-cell precursors like precursor B-cell leukemias/lymphomas (pB-ALL/LBL currently known as B-lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma (B-ALL/LL)]. The cohort included 11 leukemic presentations and 2 nodal cases, with six patients displaying L3/Burkitt-like morphology. The median age at diagnosis was 21 years (range 3–75), with a predominance in males (11 out of 13 patients). Relapse samples from three patients were also included. IG-MYC translocations involved IGH in 10 cases, IGK in 1, and IGL in 2. Notably, four cases (including the cell line 380) harbored a concurrent t(14;18)/IGH-BCL2 translocation, with a median age of 18 years (range 13–43), making transformation from an undetected follicular lymphoma unlikely. Supporting this, cell line 380 lacked mutations typically observed in follicular lymphoma. The IG-MYC rearrangements in pB-ALL/LBL were found to result from aberrant V(D)J recombination, a mechanism characteristic of early B-cell development. Most cases lacked functional B-cell receptor (BCR) expression due to biallelic IGH alterations and harbored NRAS or KRAS mutations, while mutations commonly found in BL were absent. DNA methylation profiling demonstrated that the cases clustered with precursor B cells and pB-ALL/LBL rather than with BL. These findings support the conclusion that recurrent IG-MYC translocations define a subset of pB-ALL/LBL characterized by distinct molecular features.

In this 2018 study, the authors described three rare adult cases of B-lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma (B-ALL/LBL) exhibiting Burkitt lymphoma-like morphology driven by isolated IGH/MYC translocations—a genetic abnormality typically associated with mature B-cell neoplasms. All three cases occurred in male patients presenting initially with diffuse lymphadenopathy. Cases 1 and 2 were diagnosed as B-ALL with markedly elevated lymphoblast counts in the peripheral blood and bone marrow, while Case 3, a patient with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection, was diagnosed with B-LBL based on a retroperitoneal lymph node biopsy, without bone marrow or peripheral blood involvement. Despite the Burkitt-like morphology, all cases retained an immature B-cell immunophenotype, justifying their classification as MYC-positive B-ALL/LBL. These cases are exceptionally rare, particularly in the absence of concurrent BCL2 rearrangements. The study utilized clinical assessments, flow cytometry, immunohistochemistry, fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH), and cytogenetic analyses to characterize the immunophenotype and detect MYC rearrangements. All three patients presented with aggressive clinical features, demonstrated variable responses to therapy, and ultimately had poor prognoses. The findings highlight that MYC rearrangements characterize a subtype of B-ALL/LBL with unique clinical and molecular features and unfavorable outcome.

In this 2022 study, the authors reported a rare case of atypical Burkitt leukemia/lymphoma (BL) in a 10-month-old infant, exhibiting overlapping features of both classical BL and its precursor form, preBLL. PreBLL is generally characterized by an immature B-cell immunophenotype, IGH::MYC translocations arising from aberrant V(D)J recombination, and frequent NRAS/KRAS mutations. In contrast, classical BL is associated with mature B-cell markers and recurrent mutations in MYC, ID3, and CCND3. The patient in this case demonstrated immunophenotypic immaturity, including the absence of CD20 and surface immunoglobulins, alongside BL-like morphology and an IGH::MYC rearrangement generated through V(D)J recombination. Whole-exome sequencing identified somatic mutations in FBXO11, commonly seen in classical BL, as well as TNIK and a mosaic KRAS mutation, the latter being more typical of preBLL and developmental disorders. These findings indicate a maturation stage intermediate between classical BL and preBLL. Despite the atypical molecular and phenotypic presentation, the patient achieved sustained remission following high-risk chemotherapy and remained disease-free after 38 months. This case illustrates association of IGH::MYC rearrangement with a unique type of preBLL distinct from BL.

disease.label: Embryonal Tumor With Multilayered Rosettes, C19MC-altered
Embryonal Tumor With Multilayered Rosettes, C19MC-altered

evidence.disease: Embryonal Tumor With Multilayered Rosettes, C19MC-altered
evidence.evidence_statement: This landmark study contributed to the recognition of embryonal tumor with multilayered rosettes (ETMRs) as a distinct entity in the 2016 WHO classification. Previously, ETMRs were included within the heterogeneous central nervous system-primitive neuroectodermal tumors (CNS-PNETs). ETMRs were reclassified following the identification of focal amplification at chromosome 19q13.4 encompassing a miRNA cluster (C19MC). Using DNA copy number profiling and fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH), the authors detected this amplification in 11 of 45 (~25%) primary CNS-PNETs, but in only 1 of 263 cases of non-CNS-PNETs, highlighting its specificity. In conclusion, this study provided the first molecular diagnostic marker for ETMR, a rare and aggressive pediatric brain tumor.

This study aimed to identify the mechanism underlying overexpression of a miRNA cluster on chromosome 19q13.4 (C19MC) and its oncogenicity in embryonal tumors with multilayered rosettes (ETMRs). Through analyses of 12 ETMR samples (including 2 recurrences), C19MC fusions downstream of the TTYH1 promoter were found in all cases. C19MC is the largest miRNA cluster in primates, containing 46 miRNA genes. This study found that miR-519a and miR-512-3p, encoded by the cluster, change the genome-wide methylation signature through the aberrant activation of DNMT3B, a DNA methyltransferase, to reawaken a fetal neural development program. This effect occurs through these two miRNAs targeting DNMT3B’s negative regulator RBL2. In summary, overexpression of C19MC driven by the TTYH1 promoter is the primary tumor-specific event that drives ETMR formation through its encoded oncogenic miRNAs.

This cohort study examined the molecular landscape of embryonal tumors with multilayered rosettes (ETMRs) at diagnosis and relapse. ETMRs have previously been shown to frequently (~90%) exhibit amplification or fusion of the chromosome 19 miRNA cluster (C19MC). Here, a larger cohort was analyzed, comprising 193 primary ETMR cases along with 23 matched relapse specimens. Based on the copy-number profiles inferred from methylation arrays, 90% of cases exhibited C19MC amplification. Furthermore, structural rearrangements involving C19MC were identified, with fusion partners including MYO9B on chromosome 19, MIRLET7BHG, or the previously known TTYH1. Collectively, this study presented a relatively large cohort for this rare disease; it confirmed the presence of C19MC genomic alterations in nearly all the cases, and identified several structural aberrations in C19MC through comprehensive molecular profiling.

In this 2024 case report the authors describe a case of BCR::ABL1-like B-ALL with unusual granular morphology in a female patient, 12 year old, with the following symptoms: paroxysmal headache, vomiting, but no jaundice or bleeding. CBC revealed moderate leukocytosis, 90% lymphoblast-like cells, severe anemia and normal paltelet count. Examination of peripheral blood smear revealed 87% blasts with high nucleocytoplasmic ratio, fine chromatin, and one to several nucleoli, but without Auer rods. Strickingly, most of the blasts had azurophilic granules in cytoplasm. Same blast morphology was noted during bone marrow examination with concern for granular lymphoblastic leukemia. Flow data on blood: CD45-, CD10+, CD19+ (dim), CD22+, cCD79a+, HLA-DR+, CD25+ (partial), CD34+, CD38+ (partial), MPO-, cCD3-, CD7-, CD33-, CD11c-, CD4-, CD8-, CD5-, CD7-. Karyotype was normal. FISH was negative for CRLF2, ABL1, ABL2, CSF1R rearrangements. 46-gene fusion screening by RT-PCR was negative. Copy number test (not specified) was consistent with deletions involving EBF1 (ex1-10), IKZF1 (ex1-7), PAX5 (ex2, ex5-8). Whole transcriptome sequencing detected an IGH::EPOR fusion. Based on the presence of this fusion the authors made a diagnosis of BCR::ABL1-like B-ALL. Patient received chemotherapy with VDLP (prednisone/ vincristine/ daunorubicin/ darubicin) and CAP (cyclophosphamide/ cytarabine/6 mercaptourine) with no achieving CR; switched to dexamethasone induction with improvement of WBC, then received VP (vincristine/ dexamethasone).

This is a case report from MD Anderson Cancer Center. A 40yo Caucasian male patient was diagnosed with B-ALL with IGH::EPOR fusion. The patient received 4 cycles of R-hyper-CVAD and archived CR with MRD at 0.01% by flow, followed by MUD HSCT. He relapsed 2 months s/p HSCT. Flow at RL detected 83% blasts: CD10+, CD19+, CD22+, CD34+, CD38+, CD45(dim), CD66c+, cytoplasmic CD79a+, CD123+, HLA-DR+, TdT+, CD2-, CD3-, CD4-, CD5-, CD7-, CD13-, CD14-, CD15-, CD20-, CD25-, CD33-, CD36-, CD41-, CD56-, CD64-, cytoplasmic IgM-, CRLF2-, MPO-. Chromosome analysis detected complex karyotype 45,X,-Y,add(13) (p11.2),add(17)(p11.2),-20,+21[2]/44~46,idem[cp2]/46,XY[16]. NGS revealed JAK2, KRAS, FLT3, RUNX1, and TP53 mutations. Archer FusionPlex was positive for IGH::EPOR, but FISH was negative for EPOR or IGH rearrangements or BCR::ABL1 or KMT2Ar. A diagnosis of BCR::ABL1 like B-ALL was made based on established association of EPOR rearrangements with IGH locus with this disease subtype. THe patient was treated with chemotherapy in combination with blinatumomab and achieved CR with negative MRD.

This MD Anderson Cancer Center study describes six adult patients (3 males and 3 females, median age 39 yo) with t(14;19)(q32;p13) resulting in IGH::EPOR. 3 patients did not receive any prior chemotherapy, whereas 3 presented with refractory/relapsed disease post-induction. Major symptoms at presentation: fatique, lower extremity swelling, bone pain; 3 patients had splenomegaly. No CNS involvement or extramedullary disease. The median Hb 8.8 g/dl, median PLT count 31 k/ul. All patients had circulating blasts, increased serum lactate dehydrogenase levels and serum beta-2-microglobulin level. Blast morphology: variably condensed chromatin, prominent nucleoli, agranular cytoplasm. Marrow was hypercellular for all patients, with median blast count at 90%. Flow consistent with precursor B-cell immunophenotype: CD10+, CD19+, CD20+, CD22+, CD34+, CD38+, HLA-DR+, TdT+, CD1a-, CD2-, CD3 (surface and cytoplasmic), CD4-, CD5-, CD7-, CD8-, CD14-, CD15-, CD25-, CD41-, CD56-, CD117-, MPO-. Chromosome analysis revealed t(14;19)(q32;p13) in all 6 patients, 2 patients had complex karyotype. FISH with IGH and EPOR probes showed 1F on der(14). All patients received combination chemo, but all relapsed, 5/6 died after 12 months. The manuscript describes clinical, morphologic, immunophenotypic and genetic characteristics of B-ALL caused by EPOR rearrangments with the IGH locus, which are rare primary drivers in B-ALL with BCR::ABL1 like features.

This 2021 study reports 3 adolescent/young adult patients with IGH::EPOR-positive B-ALL treated with post-induction chemotherapy combined with JAKi ruxolitinib or TKI ponatinib. Patient 1 was hispanic female (18yo) with t(14;19), negative FISH and IGH::EPOR detected by Archer FusionPlex (RNA) and DNA NGS. NGS detected partial deletion of IKZF1 and PAX5. This patient received post-induction therapy with ruxolitinib (COG AALL1521 phase II clinical trial), had complicated treatment course and persistent disease, received auto CD19 CART and archieved MRD-negative remission with HSCT from matched sibling with MRD-negative remission >3 years s/p HSCT. Patient 2 was 13 yo female with hyperdiploid karyotype (+X,+2,+5,+6,+8,+9,+10,+19,+21,+22). Archer FusionPlex detected IGH::EPOR and KRAS mutation. Her post-induction chemo was also combined with ruxolitinib with MRD<0.01%, in remission since. Patient 3 was 17yo Caucasian female with normal karyotype and IGH::EPOR by RT-PCR at diagnosis. Her consolidation therapy included cyclophoshamide, cytarabine, 6-mercaptopurine and ponatinib with complicated course. She received blinatumomab with continued ponatinib and achieved MRD negativity followed by allo HSCT.This case series summarizes clinical, morphologic, immunophenotypic and genetic characteristics of B-ALL caused by EPOR rearrangments with the IGH locus, which are rare primary drivers in B-ALL with BCR::ABL1 like features.

This 2017 study is result of collaboration of multiple institutions and was led by St. Jude Children's Research Hospital team. The total cohort of 3115 B-ALL patients (all ages) was studied, with 212 with expression profile of BCR::ABL1-like B-ALL (based on gemone and/or transcriptome sequencing). 19 out of 212 cases (8.9%) revealed 4 types of EPOR rearrangements: insertion of EPOR distal to the IGH enhancer (73.7%), insertion of EPOR into IGK at 2p11.2 (10.5%), cytogenetically visible t(14;19)(q32;p13) (10.5%), and insertion of EPOR upstream of LAIR1 (leukocyte-associated immunoglobulin-like receptor 1) at 19q13 (5.3%). The authors demonstrated that all these EPOR rearrangements resulted in truncation of the cytoplasmic tail of EPOR with preservation of Y368 tyrosine residue essential for receptor activation and loss of distal regulatory tyrosine residues (Y426, Y454, Y456, Y504) and resulted in JAK/STAT signaling activation (potential for treatment). All EPORr cases showed no expression distal to the rearrangement by ex8 specific assay (potential for screening). Interestingly, the authors used 3 EPORr cases to isolate leukemic, stem cell, progenitor, mature cell populations to test for EPORr, which was identified not only in blasts, but also in CD33+ myeloid cells (all 3 cases), myeloid progenitors (1 case), and even in normal B-cell obtained at the time of remission in 1 case. The study described genomic structure of EPOR rearrangements in B-ALL and confirmed their association with B-ALL with BCR::ABL1-like features.

evidence.disease: Acute Myeloid Leukemia With MECOM Rearrangement
evidence.evidence_statement: In this study, 17 patients with a variant pericentric inv(3) were identified from an institutional cytogenetics database, out of283 myeloid neoplasms with a MECOM rearrangement (MECOM-R) confirmed by FISH,. Patients are 13 males and 4 females, with an age range 42-85 yrs, median age 67 yrs, and diagnosed with AML (n=15), MDS (n=1) and CMML (n=1). Using metaphase FISH with commercially available MECOM dual color breakapart DNA probes, chromosomal breakpoints were identified at 3p23 (n=11), 3p25 (n=3), 3p21 (n=2) and 3p13 (n=1), in addition to the 3q26.2 breakpoint leading to MECOM-R. These pericentric inversions (inv(3)) detected by metaphase FISH were missed by initial karyotyping in 16 of the 17 cases. Somatic mutations were detected with NGS-based analysis on an 81-gene panel. Similar to classic/ paracentric inv(3)/GATA2::MECOM-R, pericentric inv(3) patients in this showed cytopenia, morphological dysplasia of megakaryocytes, -7/del(7q) and dismal outcomes (mean OS of 14 months). Unique features such as thrombocytopenia (15/17; 88%), increased monocytes in peripheral blood (15/17; 88%), and decreased megakaryocytes (11/17; 65%) were also observed. An average of 3 mutation events per case were identified in the study cohort which is higher than the average of 2 mutation events per case in classic inv(3)/t(3;3). The highest frequency of mutations was detected in gene NRAS (35%), followed by RUNX1, FLT3, ASXL1, PTPN11, SF3B1 and TP53. These 7 genes accounted for 53% of the mutation events. Mutations in SF3B1 are reported more commonly in the classic inv(3)/t(3;3) cases and were found in only 3 cases of pericentric inv(3)/MECOM-R cohort. As pericentric inv(3)s are subtle/ cryptic, reflex MECOM-R BAP FISH is recommended in myeloid neoplasms showing -7/del(7q), an aberration found at a high frequency of 75% in this study. Detection of pericentric inv(3) with MECOM-R may change the classification of the neoplasm from intermediate-risk to high-risk and the diagnosis from MDS to AML in some cases. In summary, the study shows that atypical 3q26/MECOM–R with loci in the p arm of chromosome 3 result in leukemia with the same clinical and pathology characteristics as the classical inv(3)/t(3;3)(q21q26), and may be classified together as a single entity of MECOM-rearranged AML.

evidence.disease: Acute Myeloid Leukemia With MECOM Rearrangement
evidence.evidence_statement: This study evaluates the frequency of MECOM rearrangements by fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) in 76 AML and 21 MDS patients with various 3q chromosomal aberrations. Patients were referred to four institutions in Italy (in Bologna, Ferrara, Padova, Rovigo) between 1995-2014. MECOM rearrangements were found in 51 of the 97 patients (54.8%) most of which showed 3q26 involvement by chromosome banding analysis (CBA). Of the 51 patients: 26 patients showed inv(3)/t(3;3) and 15 patients showed other balanced 3q26 translocations (t(3q26)). Of the remaining 10 patients with various 3q abnormalities (10.3%), 5 showed balanced translocations involving 3q21 or 3q25 and leading to RPN1/MECOM rearrangement, 2 showed intrachromosomal gene amplification leading to MECOM overexpression, and 3 patients were missed for 3q26 involvement by CBA due to suboptimal quality of chromosome morphology during sample preparation. All cases showed MECOM overexpression by real-time quantitative PCR. Detection of such cryptic MECOM rearrangements by FISH in this study suggests that the frequency of MECOM involvement in myeloid malignancies is underestimated. The study showed that AML with variant MECOM rearrangements has same characteristics as AML with classic inv(3)(q21q26). As MECOM rearrangements are associated with very short overall survival (OS) and poor prognosis, patients with any 3q abnormalities should be screened for MECOM rearrangement.

evidence.disease: Acute Myeloid Leukemia With MECOM Rearrangement
evidence.evidence_statement: In this study, samples from 33 patients presenting with AML or MDS were collected from either the Erasmus Hematology Department biobank (The Netherlands) or from the Munich Leukemia Laboratory (Germany). Multiple assays were used for sample characterization including metaphase karyotyping, MECOM interphase FISH,quantitative real-time PCR on mRNA, SNP array analysis, sequencing of the targeted chromosomal region 3q21.1-3q26.2 (3q-capture), RNA sequencing (RNA-seq), exome sequencing and whole genome sequencing.. 33 patients with atypical 3q26 rearrangements were identified and 25 of those showed MECOM involvement. Among these 25, losses or gains on 3q26 or on partner loci were seen in 7 cases, and no copy number losses or gains were seen in 12, indicative of balanced translocations. 4 of the 33 cases showed amplification of 3q26/MECOM by both FISH and SNP array. Overexpression of EVI1 in 30 of the 33 atypical 3q26 cases was seen, while in 29 cases MDS-EVI1 expression level was either absent or very low. The breakpoint region in 23 of the 33 cases was identified to occur either upstream (74%) or downstream (26%) of the EVI1 gene. The translocated gene partner of MECOM/3q26 was identified in 20 of the 33 cases and involved previously reported genes (THADA, CDK6, MYC and ARID1B) as well as novel and unique partner loci such as TGFBR2, HSPA8, TCF4 among others. These genes are known to be active in myeloid cells and are involved in superenhancer hijacking by the MECOM locus. These translocated enhancers contact and coactivate the promoter of EVI1 but not the promoter of MDS-EVI1. In more than 50% of the 33 cases, GATA2 expression was found to be monoallelic or skewed due to cryptic GATA2/MECOM translocation. The study concludes that both atypical 3q26/MECOM and the classical inv(3)/t(3;3)(q21q26) may be classified together as a single entity of 3q26-rearranged AMLs.
One case with presumably EGFR::USP42 fusion was mentioned in OrigiMed database of Chinese patients with lung adenocarcinoma. EGFR breakpoint in intron 27.

A 31 year old male initially thought to have a mandibular osteosarcoma that was resected and treated with adjuvant radiation and cisplatin-doxorubicin. He had a mandibular recurrence with multiple pulmonary nodules 12 months after diagnosis, at which point he underwent whole genome and whole transcriptome sequencing of their lesion. In both RNA and DNA, an in-frame deletion of exons 2-18 of ALK which retains the kinase domain and leads to activation as well as a FUS::TFCP2 fusion resulting from a rearrangements between FUS intron 6 (exons 1-6) and TFCP2 intron 1 (exons 2-15) were identified. The combination of these variants led to a change in diagnosis to an intraosseous rhabdomyosarcoma (tentatively a subtype of spindle cell rhabdomyosarcoma by WHO 2020).

profile.name: FUS::TFCP2 Fusion AND ALK Exon 2-18 Deletion

evidence.evidence_statement: A 31 year old male initially thought to have a mandibular osteosarcoma that was resected and treated with adjuvant radiation and cisplatin-doxorubicin. He had a mandibular recurrence with multiple pulmonary nodules 12 months after diagnosis, at which point he underwent whole genome and whole transcriptome sequencing of their lesion. In both RNA and DNA, an in-frame deletion of exons 2-18 of ALK which retains the kinase domain and leads to activation as well as a FUS::TFCP2 fusion resulting from a rearrangements between FUS intron 6 (exons 1-6) and TFCP2 intron 1 (exons 2-15) were identified. His cancer progressed following ifosfamide-etoposide chemotherapy and then after radiation with regorafenib, leading to hypoxic respiratory failure and mechanical ventilation. Compassionate use of alectinib was then given, resulting in dramatic clinical improvement within 48 hours, allowing him to stop ventilation. By 2 weeks there was radiological evidence of response. After 3 weeks there was new evidence of subcutaneous metastasis and pericardial involvement. The patient died of his disease 4 weeks after starting alectinib. The authors posit that this is still evidence of response but this was short lived due to the aggressiveness of the tumor and it's advanced stage at the time of treatment.

evidence.evidence_statement: The study demonstrates that EZH2 A677G is a gain-of-function mutation in B-cell lymphoma. In enzymatic assays, A677G uniquely utilized unmethylated, monomethylated, and dimethylated substrates with nearly equal efficiency. Structural modeling indicated that the A677G mutation enlarges the lysine tunnel to accommodate dimethylated substrates, while retaining the crucial Y641 residue for orienting unmethylated and monomethylated substrates. To evaluate its biological effect, the authors transiently expressed A677G in wild-type EZH2 MCF-7 cells, which resulted in marked global increases in H3K27me3 levels and a reduction in H3K27me2, relative to wild-type EZH2. These findings support the role of A677G as an activating mutation capable of altering the epigenetic landscape.

evidence.disease: Acute Myeloid Leukemia With MLL Rearrangement
evidence.evidence_statement: In this 2018 study the authors include 1,023 young people diagnosed with acute myeloid leukemia (AML). The age at presentation for the participants ranged from 0 to 29 years (median of 10 years). The presence of KMT2A rearrangements was determined from manual review of available cytogenetic results, combined with genome sequencing and RNA-sequencing findings from the study. A cytogenetic KMT2A abnormality was detected in 38% of infants (less than 3 year of age), 13% of children (aged 3 to 14 years), and 11% of adolescent and young adults (aged 15 to 29 years). Multiple KMT2A fusion partners were detected, with MLLT3 occurring most frequently. The study illustrates that KMT2A rearrangements define a subtype of AML common in children and young adults.

evidence.evidence_statement: In this 2024 study the authors included patient data from 1256 children (aged less than 19 years) across 15 different countries diagnosed with KMT2A rearranged acute myeloid leukemia (AML). KMT2A rearrangements were detected by cytogenetics, with some confirmed by fluorescence in situ hybridization, or reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction, within the local centers. Multiple KMT2A fusion partners were detected, with KMT2A::MLLT3 (n = 544, 43.3%), KMT2A::MLLT10 (n = 218, 17.4%), KMT2A::AFDN (n = 92, 7.3%), and KMT2A::ELL (n = 75, 6.0%) most frequent, together accounting for around 75% of cases. The authors found that different fusion partners, morphology and/or additional cytogenetic abnormalities may impact outcomes.

evidence.disease: Acute Myeloid Leukemia With MLL Rearrangement
evidence.evidence_statement: In this 2023 publication the authors include 3401 KMT2A rearranged leukemia samples obtained from different diagnostic centers worldwide, and subject them to DNA sequence analyses. Of these patients, 1116 were diagnosed with acute myeloid leukemia (AML), including 197 patients aged less than 12 months, 465 patients aged 1 to 18 years and 441 patients older than 18 years (for 13 patients age was unknown). AML patients displayed a diverse number of partner genes with MLLT3 (n = 339; 30.4%) and MLLT10 (n = 209; 18.7%) the most common. KMT2A rearrangements typically involve in-frame fusions with KMT2A as the 5' partner and KMT2A breakpoints in AML patients almost always occur somewhere between intron 7 and exon 13 (NM_001412597.1). KMT2A-partial tandem in-frame duplications that involve the N-terminus can also occur, mostly frequently in AML in adult patients.

The is a cytogenetic case study of a 10-year-old female with pure pigmented dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans (DFSP), also called Bednar tumor, on her right shoulder. Karyotype of tumor cells was 47,XX with 2 copies of der(22)t(17;22)(q22;q13). BAC clones mapping to 22q13.1 at the PDGFB locus, and 17q21.33 at the COL1A1I locus and used as FISH probes detected COL1A1-PDGFB gene fusion on the derivative der(22) chromosomes. RT-PCR and Sanger sequencing narrowed down the fusion to exon 41 of COL1A1 and exon 2 of PDGFB. Adult Bednar and DFSP tumors typically show ring chromosomes composed of der(22) material, while pediatric DFSP tumors show a linear structural abnormality of an unbalanced translocation t(17;22)(q22;q13). This is the first reported pediatric case of a pure Bednar tumor with a linear chromosomal structural abnormality involving chromosomes 22 and 17, in addition to having a normal chromosome 22 and two normal chromosomes 17. The COL1A1 breakpoint at exon 41 in the COL1A1-PDGFB fusion gene is newly reported in this case study and reaffirms the known variability in COL1A1 breakpoints spanning exons 6-49.

The authors studied 27 archival formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) samples of dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans (DFSP) cases obtained from Texas Children's Hospital and University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center. The cases included 16 females and 11 males with an age range of 1-73 years and diagnosed with DFSP and diffuse expression of CD34 by immunohistochemistry. Using a highly sensitive multiplex RT-PCR-direct sequencing assay developed for FFPE tissue, the authors detected COL1A1-PDGFB fusion transcripts with 18 different COL1A1 forward primers spanning the α-helical domain (exons 5-49) and a single PDGFB reverse primer. Break-apart FISH was performed using BAC DNA clones mapping centromeric and telomeric of the PGDFB locus. Sequencing analysis confirmed in-frame fusion of exon 2 of PDGFB to different breakpoints in COL1A1 (exons 7, 10, 29, 40, 46, and 49 and introns between exons 13:14, 26:27, 30:31, 33:34, 43:44, 45:46, 46:47). Of these, COL1A1 breakpoints in exon 49 and in introns between exons 13:14 and 30:31, are novel. Using both RT-PCR and FISH techniques, the authors report a higher prevalence of COL1A1-PDGFB rearrangements (96%) in DFSP cases than reported in earlier studies, and attribute this to the high sensitivity of their multiplex RT-PCR direct sequencing assay. Testing FFPE specimen with both FISH and RT-PCR would prove helpful for the differential diagnosis of atypical, fibrosarcomatous and metastatic DFSP.

In this study, paraffin-embedded tissue microarray (TMA) evaluation of translocation t(17;22)(q22;q13) was performed on 40 tissue samples from 24 female and 16 male DFSP patients (37 primary tumors, 3 local recurrences) obtained from 3 hospitals in Barcelona, Spain. The median age of these DFSP patients was 43 y and the age range was 15-87 y. A second tissue microarray included 20 samples from dermatofibroma (DF) patients. Samples from 6 postsurgical scars were used as negative controls. FISH was performed using dual-color dual-fusion BAC clones to detect the cytogenetic COL1A1-PDGFB translocation. From the evaluable 29 DFSP cases, 86% (n=25) showed the COL1A1-PDGFB FISH signal pattern, which was absent in all DF control cases and in the 6 scars. Of these 25 COL1A1-PDGFB positive DFSP cases, 19 showed multiple (more than 3) copies of the translocation. Tumor size correlated positively with a higher proportion of DFSP tumor cells showing the fusion signal, and DFSPs with fibrosarcomatous areas (DFSP-FS) also showed cells with 6 or more COL1A1-PDGFB gene fusions signals.

This study provided in vivo evidence showing the adipocyte-specific oncogenicity of the FUS::CHOP fusion transcript in liposarcoma, using a transgenic mouse model with ubiquitous FUS::CHOP expression driven by the elongation factor 1a (EF1a) promoter. These mice uniformly developed liposarcoma without sex bias and exhibited characteristic symptoms similar to those in human liposarcoma. No tumors were detected in other tissues. Mechanistically, FUS::CHOP expression in vivo blocked adipocyte differentiation by inducing the expression of the nuclear receptor peroxisome proliferative-activated receptor gamma (PPARg). The study provides evidence that the FUS::DDIT3 fusion acts as the primary oncogenic driver in myxoid liposarcoma (MLS) and is thus a suitable diagnostic marker for this tumor type.

This preclinical study examined the effect of the FUS::DDIT3 fusion protein on the oncogenic role of IGF-1R/PI3K/Akt signaling in myxoid liposarcoma (MLS) and explored the therapeutic potential of IGF-1R inhibitors, including NVP-AEW541 in this disease. Immunohistochemistry (IHC) revealed elevated expression and activating phosphorylation of various components in the IGF-1R signaling pathway in MLS clinical specimens (n=60). Overexpression of FUS::DDIT3 in HT1080 fibrosarcoma cells induced IGF2-IGF-1R/PI3K/Akt activation. Topical administration of NVP-AEW541 onto MLS xenograft tumors on the chick chorioallantoic membrane (CAM) was found to significantly suppress tumor growth in vivo (p<0.05). The study shows that the FUS::DDIT3 fusion drives oncogenic program in MLS; it is a defining abnormality and a suitable diagnostic marker for this tumor type.

evidence.disease: B-lymphoblastic Leukaemia/lymphoma With Other Defined Genetic Alterations
evidence.evidence_statement: In this retrospective multicenter study, 218 patients diagnosed with B-lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma (B-ALL) harboring ZNF384 rearrangements were analyzed between 1992 and 2018 across 16 international consortia. ZNF384 rearrangements were found in about 5% of pediatric and 10% of adult B-ALL cases and were mutually exclusive with other well-defined genetic subtypes. FISH), RT-PCR, and NGS identified ZNF384 fusion transcripts with partners such as EP300, TCF3, TAF15, and CREBBP. Detection of ZNF384 fusions was critical for classifying B-ALL cases lacking other recurrent cytogenetic abnormalities. EP300::ZNF384 fusions showed a distinct clinical profile, including older age at diagnosis and favorable outcomes, while other ZNF384 rearrangements exhibited unique immunophenotypic features like aberrant myeloid marker expression (CD13, CD33). These findings highlight the diagnostic importance of ZNF384 rearrangements in B-ALL and support their recognition as a distinct molecular entity.

evidence.evidence_statement: In this study, the authors investigated a targeted diagnostic approach to identify ZNF384 rearrangements in B-lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma (B-ALL) based on immunophenotypic features. Since ZNF384 fusions are often cryptic and linked to dim CD10 expression and aberrant CD13/CD33 expression, 109 B-ALL patients with <80% CD10 expression and negative BCR-ABL1 status were screened. ZNF384 rearrangements were found in 14 cases, with EP300::ZNF384 as the most common fusion. Flow cytometry screening, FISH followed by RT-PCR and Sanger sequencing identified further fusion partners including EP300, TAF15, and TCF3. Recognizing ZNF384 fusions is particularly valuable for diagnosing B-ALL cases that do not harbor other defining cytogenetic or molecular alterations.

A cross-sectional cohort study was performed in 161 men with metastatic prostate cancer undergoing a change in treatment to determine if pre-therapy AR-V7 nuclear protein expression in circulating tumor cells (CTCs) is a treatment-specific marker for outcomes between androgen receptor signaling (ARS) inhibitors and taxanes. A multivariable model adjusting for baseline factor associated with survival showed superior overall survival with taxanes relative to ARS inhibitors when AR-V7-positive CTCs were detected pre-therapy (hazard ratio , 0.24; 95% CI 0.10-0.57; P=0.035).

A blinded, multi-institutional cohort study was performed in 142 men with metastatic, castration-resistant prostate cancer to determine if pre-therapy nuclear-localized expression of AR-V7 protein in circulating tumor cells (CTCs) is a treatment-selective marker for outcome following treatment with either androgen receptor signaling (ARS) inhibitors or taxanes. Patients with AR-V7-positive CTCs had superior overall survival with taxanes vs ARS inhibitors (hazard ratio 0.62; 95% CI 0.28-1.39; P=.25). Patients with AR-V7-negative CTCs had superior overall survival with ARS inhibitors vs taxanes (hazard ratio 1.67; 95 CI 1.00-2.81); P=.05).

To compare the activity of AR-V7 with that of full-length AR (AR-FL) lentiviral stable cell lines of castrate-resistant prostate cancer were generated that expressed doxycycline-regulated AR-V7 or AR-FL using the cell line C4-2 PCa. These cells were injected into the tibias of castrated male mice. Compared to cells expressing or over-expressing AR-FL those expressing AR-V7 induced mixed osteoblastic/osteoclastic bone lesions and increased the area of bone lesions 4-6 weeks after injection. Expression of SOX9 protein, a known driver of metastasis, increased significantly in tumors expressing AR-V7 but remained low and unchanged in those expressing AR-FL.
