Two novel somatic interstitial in-frame deletions in RET, with unknown transformation potential, were identified in medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) tumor samples. One of these (RET E632_L633del) was compared to already established variants (as positive controls) including RET M918T, which authors describe as typical of MEN2B phenotype familial MTC and as a frequent somatic mutation in sporadic MTC. In-vitro transforming activity was tested using focus formation assays on NIH3T3 cells. Vectors for control, M918T, and E632_L633del with neomycin resistance were made and expressed in NIH3T3, and selection with G418 performed. 1.4 x 10^4 M918T and 9.6 x 10^3 control colonies (colonies/ug DNA used in transfection) survived G418 selection. 1.8 x 10^2 transformed loci formed for M918T cells, but <1 x 10^–2 formed for wildtype control. This ratio was 0.013 transformed loci per M918T colony.

profile.name: RET M918T
profile.summary: RET M918T is the most common somatically acquired mutation in medullary thyroid cancer (MTC). While there currently are no RET-specific inhibiting agents, promiscuous kinase inhibitors have seen some success in treating RET overactivity. Data suggests however, that the M918T mutation may lead to drug resistance, especially against the VEGFR-inhibitor motesanib. It has also been suggested that RET M918T leads to more aggressive MTC with a poorer prognosis.

evidence.evidence_statement: A total of 56 metastatic medullary thyroid cancer cases (50 sporadic, 6 familial) were analyzed for RET mutations. A total of 7 cases were found to have a RET germline mutations however one case had a mutation previously shown to have low transforming potential and was considered sporadic. 34/50 sporadic cases had M918T mutations and 3/6 familial cases carried a RET M918T germline mutation. All three showed local recurrences/metastases, and one had instances of pheochromocytoma.

Across treated patients (200 mg-random n = 91; 300 mg-all n = 111), grade ≥3 treatment related AEs occurred in 40.7% and 58.6%, most commonly diarrhea (2.2% vs 18.0%), blood CPK increase (6.6% vs 12.6%), and anemia (4.4% vs 6.3%), with no treatment related deaths; both dose levels met the prespecified primary endpoint of IRC confirmed ORR.

The use of circulating tumor DNA in blood for TMB assessment was tested. The cancer gene panel NCC-GP150, which covers the whole exon regions of 150 genes, was created and tested for correlation against established methods for TMB assessment. Testing compared whole exome sequencing (WES) results from tissue samples of 48 Chinese advanced NSCLC patients with NCC-GP150 from matched blood samples from those patients. A Spearman correlation of 0.62 (P<0.001) was reported between these results, when the cutoff between high and low blood TMB (H-bTMB) was greater or equal to 6. In a test with 33 different cancer types, NCC-GP150 correlated strongly with established WES results in 25/33 of the tumor types. 50 advanced NSCLC patients were treated with PD-1 or PDL-1 inhibition. When the H-bTMB cutoff was set to 6, then a minimum hazard ratio favoring H-bTMB patients was seen of HR=0.39 (0.18-0.84) P=.02. For the subset of patients with anti-PD1/PD-L1 therapy as first- or second-Line treatment, results were stronger with HR=0.08 (0.02-0.36) P=.001 at a cutoff of H-bTMB of 6. In this subgroup overall response rate was significantly different (P=0.003), 61.1% in H-b-TMB and 6.7% in L-bTMB. Additionally, in responders bTMB was significantly higher (median 10) than in non responders (median 5, P=0.008). The authors conclude that ctDNA-based bTMB measured using the NCC-GP150 panel is a potential biomarker for anti–PD-1 and anti–PD-L1 treatment in NSCLC.

In this 2022 study, the authors included 40 patients aged ≤12 months diagnosed with spindle cell rhabdomyosarcoma (SCRMS) enrolled in international trials and registries, of whom 39 presented with localized disease. FISH or RT-PCR was utilized to investigate VGLL2 and NCOA2 gene fusions. Among 26 tumors with available molecular evaluation, VGLL2 and/or NCOA2 gene rearrangements were detected in 13 (50%) cases. These included NCOA2-VGLL2 fusions in 2 tumours, NCOA2-related fusions (TEAD1-NCOA2) in 5, and VGLL2-related fusions (VGLL2-CITED2) in 6. No gene fusion was identified in 12 cases, and the remaining 14 cases were not tested or had insufficient tissue. The cohort was composed of 18 females and 21 males, with a median age at diagnosis of 2.5 months. The authors concluded that they have identified a subset of spindle cell rhabdomyosarcoma occurring in infants, in which recurrent VGLL2 and NCOA2 gene fusions are present in half of the cases with available molecular data, supporting their role in the biology of infantile SCRMS.

In this 2013 study, the authors included 21 spindle cell and sclerosing rhabdomyosarcomas (RMS), and a control group of 4 embryonal RMS and 3 ectomesenchymomas. RNA sequencing and FISH were utilized to investigate NCOA2 gene abnormalities. NCOA2 gene rearrangements were detected in 3 of the 10 pediatric spindle cell RMS (in a 4-week-old, 3-month-old, and 7-month-old) and not detected in any of the tumors from older children, adults, sclerosing RMS, or the control group. SRF::NCOA2 fusions were present in one tumor, and TEAD1::NCOA2 fusions were identified in another, with RT-PCR confirming fusion of SRF exon 6 with NCOA2 exon 12 in the first case. The cohort was composed of 2 females and 1 male, all under one year of age, with tumors arising in the chest wall or posterior neck. The authors concluded that they have identified a subset of spindle cell rhabdomyosarcoma occurring almost exclusively in infants, characterized by recurrent NCOA2 gene rearrangements, which distinguishes it from morphologically similar tumors in older patients.

In the phase I study of pazopanib and vorinostat in 36 patients with advanced solid tumors, detection of hotspot TP53 mutation was associated with a higher rate of SD ≥6 months/PR, longer median PFS (months), and longer median OS (months) compared to patients without a hotspot TP53 mutation. In colorectal cancer cases, detected TP53 hotspot mutations included TP53 R213*, TP53 G245S, and TP53 R273C. In the subgroup of patients with metastatic colorectal cancer and sarcoma treated with pazopanib and vorinostat, those with detected hotspot TP53 mutations (n = 6) had a significantly longer median PFS of 6.5 months (95% CI 3.0–9.0; p = 0.023) compared to 2.0 months (95% CI 1.8–2.2; p = 0.023) in TP53-undetected cases (n = 10), and a significantly longer median OS of 19.8 months (95% CI 8.2–31.4; p = 0.021) versus 7.2 months (95% CI 0.6–13.8; p = 0.021), respectively.

evidence.disease: Round Cell Sarcoma With EWSR1-non-ETS Fusion
evidence.evidence_statement: This case series study reported 11 neoplasms harboring the EWSR1::PATZ1 gene fusion with 7 in the soft tissue and 4 in the brain. Paired-end sequencing identified a somatic intra-chromosomal paracentric inversion on chromosome 22 involving EWSR1 and PATZ1, located ~2 Mb apart, in all cases. This rearrangement permits transcription of both genes in the same orientation. Two soft tissue cases,1 myoepithelial carcinoma and 1 undifferentiated low-grade sarcoma, were further characterized by RT-PCR with Sanger sequencing. In the former case, EWSR1 exon 8 was fused to PATZ1 exon 1 with a 28-nucleotide insertion derived from EWSR1 intron 8 encoding 10 amino acids. In the latter case, EWSR1 exon 8 was also fused to PATZ1 exon 1, with concurrent presence of an in-frame deletion within exon 1 sequence. Further comprehensive molecular profiling revealed loss/deletion of CDKN2A/CDKN2B in 5 of 7 soft tissue cases (71.4%), with 1 showing concurrent MDM2 amplification. This study expanded the evidence for the recurrent EWSR1::PATZ1 fusion in small round cell sarcoma.

evidence.evidence_statement: This case series study presented clinical, histopathological, and molecular findings of 9 EWSR1::PATZ1-rearranged sarcomas, including one previously reported case. The cohort included 4 males and 5 females ranging in age from 10 to 81 years. These tumors most occurred in the thoracoabdominal soft tissues (5 in abdominal wall soft tissues, 3 in the thorax, 1 in the posterior neck). Molecularly, the EWSR1 (exon8)::PATZ1(exon 1) gene fusion, with or without the inclusion of part of EWSR1 intron 8, was identified in all cases by NGS. Select cases were subjected to FISH analyses. All 4 tested cases (8/100 nuclei in 3 cases; 9/100 nuclei in 1 case) showed EWSR1 break-apart signals, yet none reached the diagnostic cutoff (10% positive nuclei). Combined FISH and NGS analyses further revealed CDKN2A homozygous or heterozygous deletion in 3 of 6 cases. Chart review and pathological examination showed diverse clinical courses and a broad morphologic spectrum. Collectively, EWSR1::PATZ1 sarcomas are clinically and morphologically heterogeneous diseases, and FISH is an suboptimal for the detection of the EWSR1 rearrangement in this disease.

evidence.evidence_statement: This study presented molecular and clinicopathologic findings of a cohort of 17 EWSR1::PATZ1 soft tissue sarcomas. These tumors occurred in 12 males and 5 females with 15-71 years of age (median age, 50 years) and involved the thoracoabdominal soft tissues (14 cases; 82%), lower extremities (2 cases; 12%), and tongue (1 case; 6%). Targeted RNA sequencing identified EWSR1::PATZ1 gene fusions in all cases, with variable breakpoints located within exon 7-9 of EWSR1, with exon 8 being the predominant breakpoint (14/17, 82%), fused to exon 1 of PATZ1. Genomic breakpoints were obtained from 12 cases showing multiple junction configurations of the EWSR1::PATZ1 gene fusion at the genomic level. The study also showed broad morphological features with more favorable outcome than previously described for EWSR1::PATZ1 positive sarcomas. Notably, this study had two times more male than female patients, although no male predominance had been described previously for the EWSR1::PATZ1 fusion sarcomas.

In this 2015 study, formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissue samples were retrieved from the diagnostic pathology archives of the Royal National Orthopaedic Hospital (RNOH) and the Basel Bone Tumour Reference Centre (BBTRC). All cases were reviewed by specialist bone tumour pathologists and classified according to World Health Organization (WHO) criteria. To investigate the oncogenic driver of Giant Cell Tumour of Bone (GCT), whole-genome sequencing was performed on five cases and whole-exome sequencing on one case. In addition, targeted hotspot sequencing using a 14-gene panel, including H3F3A and H3F3B, was conducted to assess the specificity of the p.G34W alteration. This analysis included 91 GCTs and 321 other osteoclast-rich bone lesions. No driver mutations other than the H3F3A p.G34W mutation were identified in the sequenced genomes and exome. Targeted sequencing detected this mutation in 83 GCT cases, with single cases of H3F3A p.G34R and p.G34M; no mutations were found in H3F3B. Both GCTs that metastasized to the lung harbored the H3F3A p.G34W mutation. Overall, H3F3A p.G34 alterations were present in 96% (85/89) of GCTs and absent in other bone tumours in this cohort, supporting their role as highly sensitive and specific molecular markers for GCT.

In this 2015 study, formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tumor samples diagnosed between 1996 and 2014 as giant cell tumor of bone (GCTB), chondroblastoma, chondromyxoid fibroma, aneurysmal bone cyst, or telangiectatic osteosarcoma were retrieved from the Leiden University Medical Centre. A total of 75 GCTB samples were analyzed, including 15 recurrences from 12 patients. H3F3A hotspot mutations were assessed using Sanger sequencing, and immunohistochemistry for H3K36 trimethylation and ATRX expression was performed to evaluate correlation with mutation status. H3F3A G34W/V mutations were identified in 41 of 59 GCTBs (69%) (39 G34W, 2 G34V). Rare variants included a G34 stop codon and a TCT insertion at position 35. H3K36 trimethylation was present in 59 of 60 cases and was more frequent in mutated tumors, whereas ATRX loss showed no correlation with mutation status. Only G34W/V variants were considered mutation-positive for correlation analysis due to the uncertain significance of other variants. In conclusion, H3F3A mutation analysis (particularly G34W/V) by Sanger sequencing represents a highly specific, though less sensitive, diagnostic tool for distinguishing GCTB from other giant cell–containing bone tumors.

In this study, the authors investigated a case of pseudomyogenic hemangioendothelioma in a 33-year-old woman presenting with multifocal lytic bone lesions. Previous studies had demonstrated recurrent SERPINE1::FOSB and ACTB::FOSB fusions in pseudomyogenic hemangioendothelioma; however, this tumor lacked those known rearrangements. Using RNA sequencing, RT-PCR, and Sanger sequencing, the authors identified a novel in-frame WWTR1::FOSB fusion, joining exon 4 of WWTR1 (3q25) to exon 2 of FOSB (19q13). The fusion transcript places FOSB under the control of the WWTR1 promoter and is predicted to encode a 553-amino-acid chimeric WWTR1::FOSB transcription factor. Immunohistochemistry demonstrated strong nuclear FOSB expression in the tumor cells, supporting fusion-driven overexpression. Cytogenetic analysis showed a normal karyotype, highlighting the utility of RNA-based methods in detecting cryptic rearrangements. The authors conclude that, in addition to SERPINE1::FOSB and ACTB::FOSB, WWTR1::FOSB represents another recurrent FOSB-related fusion in pseudomyogenic hemangioendothelioma. Detection of FOSB rearrangements and associated nuclear FOSB overexpression may serve as a valuable diagnostic marker to distinguish pseudomyogenic hemangioendothelioma from its histologic mimics.

In this 2017 study the authors included four cases of gastroblastoma with control cases of histologic mimics. Gastroblastoma patients were aged 9, 27, 28 and 56 years. RNASeq identified a MALAT1::GLI1 fusion in two gastroblastomas, with MALAT1 exon 1 fusing to GLI1 exons 5 or 6, and RT-PCR confirming the presence of the fusion. FISH was positive for rearrangement and fusion of the MALAT1 and GLI1 loci in all four cases. Of the contols, one plexiform fibromyxoma was positive for MALAT1 rearrangement but negative for GLI1 rearrangement, with all other controls negative for MALAT1::GLI1. Pathway analysis on differentially expressed genes identified upregulation of the Sonic hedgehog pathway. The authors conclude that gastroblastoma should exist as a distinct entity characterized by the presence of a somatic, recurrent, oncogenic MALAT1::GLI1 fusion gene.

In this 2023 case study the authors investigate a tumour with biphasic morphology composed of epithelial and spindle cell components, diagnosed in a 29-year-old woman. RT-PCR analysis revealed that the tumor harbored the MALAT1::GLI1 fusion gene. The authors also summarised the 16 cases of gastroblastoma that have been reported in the literature, with the MALAT::GLI1 fusion gene identified in 5 of these cases, with testing not performed in 9 cases and the 2 remaining cases showing EWSR1::CTBP1 and PTCH1::GLI2 fusions. They conclude that they have identified another case for this rare entity and postulate the potential role of targeted therapeutics, as nuclear expression of PD-L1 and HDAC2 was observed.

In this 2019 case study the authors investigate a gastric antral tumor with morphological, immunophenotypic and genotypic features consistent with gastroblastoma in a 79-year-old male. Molecular analysis identified a MALAT1::GLI1 fusion gene that retained exon 6 of GLI1. A previous "paraganglioma" detected in the patient was also found to harbor the MALAT1::GLI1 gene fusion, hence the present tumor was assumed to represent the relapse of a disease that ﬁrst presented at 74 years. The authors conclude that they have another example of a gastroblastoma, which is exceedingly rare, and have extended the known age range that this tumor can occur.

This exploratory analysis of the Phase 3 MYSTIC trial (NCT02453282) evaluated blood tumour mutational burden (bTMB) as a predictive biomarker for first-line durvalumab with or without tremelimumab vs chemotherapy in patients with advanced or metastatic non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). The cfDNA assay used was GuardantOMNI (500 genes, 2.145 Mb) and the bTMB was calculated by identifying somatic synonymous and non-synonymous single nucleotide variants (SNVs) and short insertions/deletions (indels) at all variant allele frequencies. Pre-treatment plasma bTMB demonstrated a positive correlation with the patient-paired tissue TMB (tTMB) (Spearman rank correlation = 0.6, n=352). In the population evaluable for bTMB (n= 809), patients with bTMB ≥20 mut/Mb showed improved overall survival (OS) for durvalumab plus tremelimumab vs chemotherapy (median, 21.9 months vs 10.0 months; unadjusted HR, 0.49). The improved OS for durvalumab plus tremelimumab vs chemotherapy was not observed in patients with bTMB < 20 mut/Mb. Similarly, bTMB ≥20 mut/Mb, but not <20 mut/Mb, was also associated with improved PFS and ORR for durvalumab plus tremelimumab vs chemotherapy. These findings support a bTMB threshold of 20 mut/Mb as predictive of optimal clinical benefit in OS, PFS, and ORR for durvalumab with tremelimumab.

profile.summary: Tumors with a high mutational burden (TMB-High) are reported to have increased sensitivity to immunotherapy. High Tumor Mutation Burden is defined as 10 or more mutations per MB of DNA in an FDA approved companion diagnostic test based on next generation sequencing.

evidence.evidence_statement: In ovarian carcinoma (OVCA) preclinical models, CCNE1 amplification predicted synergistic sensitivity to lunresertib (RP-6306) + camonsertib (RP-3500). CCNE1 copy number correlates with synergy by MTT assay (R² = 0.87, p = 0.0064) and ~80% growth inhibition at low-dose combination (RP-6306 31 nM + RP-3500 7.8 nM) in CCNE1-overexpressing cells. The sensitive CCNE1-amplified OVCA cell lines were OVCAR3, FUOV1, COV318 (CN>5) and CCNE1 copy gain were OVCAR8, OVSAHO (CN 2-5). In CCNE1-amplified OVCA PDX models (WO-19, WO-77), combination treatment (RP-6306 5–10 mg/kg + RP-3500 5 mg/kg) significantly increased tumor suppression and improved survival. This method of treatment also reduced metastases vs monotherapy (WO-19 metastases p = 0.0401 and p = 0.0122), with tumor progression (tumor volume > 1000 mm³) as the primary endpoint.

In the breast carcinoma cohort of the phase II TAPUR trial (NCT02693535), patients with BRCA1/2 alterations treated with olaparib (26 evaluable) had 1 CR (BRCA2 loss), 11 PR (BRCA1 n=5, BRCA2 n=4, BRCA1/2 n=2), 6 SD16+ (BRCA1 n=1, BRCA2 n=4, BRCA1/2 n=1) yielding ORR 46% (95% CI, 27-67) and DCR 69% (90% CI 55-100; p < 0.001 vs null 15%). Median PFS was 26 weeks (95% CI 15–33) and median OS 55 weeks (95% CI 33–100) in this cohort. Across all TAPUR cohorts combined (NCT02693535; n = 116 evaluable; BC n = 26, BTC n = 18, LC n = 25, UC n = 15, HP n = 32), patients with advanced solid tumors harboring BRCA1/2 alterations treated with olaparib achieved 13 CR, 15 PR, 20 SD≥16 weeks, and 68 PD, corresponding to an ORR of 24% (95% CI 17–33). The median duration of response was 31 weeks (range 7–284). Among patients with recent platinum exposure (n = 81), 43% achieved DC, including 15 OR (19%; 95% CI 11–29) and 20 SD16+ (25%; 95% CI 16–36).

An 8-year-old girl presented with secondary BRAF V600-mutant histiocytic sarcoma following T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia. After the poor response to initial salvage chemotherapy, the patient responded well to dabrafenib and trametinib combination therapy and remained in partial remission with no disease progression for 3 years.

profile.name: BRAF V600
profile.summary: BRAF mutations of the valine 600 residue have been shown to be recurrent in many cancer types. Of the V600 mutations, V600E is the most widely researched. V600 mutations as a whole have been correlated to poorer prognosis in colorectal and papilarry thyroid cancers. V600 mutations have also been shown to confer sensitivity to the BRAF inhibitor dabrafenib. For a more detailed summary, click the individual mutations.

evidence.evidence_statement: In this 2019 study, targeted RNA sequencing using the Archer FusionPlex technology was validated and implemented to detect oncogenic fusion transcripts in 62 genes recurrently rearranged in solid tumors, including sarcomas, without prior knowledge of fusion partners. A total of 192 formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) bone and soft tissue tumor samples from January 2016 to January 2018 were submitted to Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center for analysis. In-frame gene fusions were identified in 79 of 184 cases (43%), including 6 cases (3%) with novel fusion partners. In two cases of pseudomyogenic hemangioendothelioma present in this study cohort the testing revealed FOSB fusions with a novel partner gene ACTB. In both ACTB::FOSB fusion positive pseudomyogenic hemangioendothelioma cases the ACTB exon 3 was joined with the FOSB exon 2. The FOSB breakpoint in the ACTB::FOSB fusion matched previously reported breakpoints. This study further confirms specific association between FOSB fusions and pseudomyogenic hemangioendothelioma.

This is part of a multi-centred, randomised, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial, CHOICE-01, that examined therapeutic response to first-line chemotherapy plus PD-1 inhibitor in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients to explore ctDNA-based stratification strategies. 405 treatment-naïve patients with either locally advanced or metastatic NSCLC that do not carry EGFR or ALK driver mutations were randomly assigned to receive toripalimab (n=309) or placebo (n = 156) in combination with chemotherapy. 371 of the 405 patients with pre-treatment ctDNA present (maximal somatic allele frequency of >=0.5%). Blood-based TMB (bTMB) measured by the 520-gene OncoCompass Plus panel (Burning Rock Biotech) was calculated as the number of small single-nucleotide variations (SNVs) and indels detected at an allele frequency of >=0.2% per Mb of coding regions of target genes (1.003 Mb for the panel used). Using 13 mutations/ Mb (top 20%) as the cut off, patients with high bTMB achieved greater progression free survival from chemotherapy plus PD-1 inhibitor compare dot the bTMB-low group (interaction p = 0.027). However, no difference in overall survival benefits from the addition of PD-1 inhibitor was observed between the two groups.

evidence.evidence_statement: This is part of a open-label phase 3 trial, NEPTUNE, that examined therapeutic response to first-line durvalumab plus tremelimumab in patients with metastatic non-small cel lung cancer (NSCLC). 823 patiehts with metastatic NSCLC that do not carry EGFR or ALK driver mutations were randomly assigned to receive first-line durvalumab (20 mg/kg every 4 weeks until progression) plus tremelimumab (1 mg/kg every 4 weeks for up to four doses) or standard platinum-based chemotherapy. Blood-based TMB (bTMB) was evaluated in 512 patients.bTMB measured by the 500 gene Guardant OMNI plasma next-generation sequencing (NGS) platform was calculated as the number of synonymous and non-synonymous small single-nucleotide variations (SNVs) and short indels detected at all allele fractions per Mb of coding regions of target genes. Among the bTMB-high patients (>= 20 mut/ Mb) (n = 129), no statistically significant overall survival (OS) (HR 0.71 [95% CI: 0.49–1.05]; median OS, 11.7 versus 9.1 months) or progression free survival (PFS) (HR 0.77 [95% CI: 0.51–1.15]) improvement was observed with durvalumab plus tremelimumab (n = 69) compared to chemotherapy (n = 60). In the exploratory analysis of bTMB with various cutoffs (8-28 mut/Mb), OS and PFS analysis demonstrated an association between higher bTMB and improved hazard ratios for durvalumab plus tremelimumab compared to chemotherapy. Tissue TMB (tTMB) was also evaluated in 369 of the patients. tTMB measured by the 324 gene FoundationOne CDx platform was calculated as the number of synonymous and non-synonymous small single-nucleotide variations (SNVs) and short indels per Mb of coding regions of target genes. In the exploratory analysis of tTMB with various cutoffs (4-18 mut/Mb), OS and PFS analysis demonstrated an association between higher bTMB and improved hazard ratios for durvalumab plus tremelimumab compared to chemotherapy. Among the 236 patients with matched plasma and tissue samples, moderate correlation was observed between bTMB and tTMB (Spearman’s rho = 0.64; Pearson’sr = 0.80). In conclusion, this study did not meet its primary end point of statistically significant improved OS with durvalumab plus tremelimumab compared to chemotherapy among bTMB-high mNSCLC patients. The authors noted that despite this study being limited by altered study design and therefore a small size of the primary analysis population, the therapeutic activity was consistent with observations in previous studies and aligned with expected outcomes based on underlying biological mechanisms.

evidence.evidence_statement: In a study of 100 patients with sporadic medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC), RET gene exons 10-11 and 13-16 were analyzed with tumor and matched normal samples. A somatic RET mutation was identified in 43% of cases and of these 79% (34/43) were M918T mutations.

profile.name: RET M918T
profile.summary: RET M918T is the most common somatically acquired mutation in medullary thyroid cancer (MTC). While there currently are no RET-specific inhibiting agents, promiscuous kinase inhibitors have seen some success in treating RET overactivity. Data suggests however, that the M918T mutation may lead to drug resistance, especially against the VEGFR-inhibitor motesanib. It has also been suggested that RET M918T leads to more aggressive MTC with a poorer prognosis.

evidence.evidence_statement: In this 2017 study, the authors characterized 284 cases of Philadelphia chromosome-like acute lymphoblastic leukemia (Ph-like ALL) identified from a cohort of 1,389 pediatric patients with high-risk B-ALL. This subtype is defined by a gene expression profile similar to BCR::ABL1-positive ALL but lacks that canonical fusion, and is associated with a diverse array of genetic alterations activating cytokine receptor and tyrosine kinase signaling. The cohort showed a male predominance (57.4%) and was enriched for older age and high white blood cell counts. Comprehensive molecular profiling, including reverse transcriptase PCR and transcriptome sequencing, identified targetable kinase alterations in 83.8% of the Ph-like ALL cases. Among these, fusions involving the LYN kinase gene were identified as rare, recurrent oncogenic drivers within this high-risk subtype. The study reported one case harboring a novel GATAD2A::LYN fusion. This fusion retains the tyrosine kinase domain of LYN and is predicted to activate SRC-family kinase signaling. The expression profile of this LYN-fusion-positive case was classified as Ph-like, definitively supporting its biological and diagnostic classification within the BCR::ABL1-like disease spectrum.

This retrospective Japanese multicenter study investigated kinase-activating gene fusions in pediatric B-lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL) lacking recurrent cytogenetic abnormalities, with the goal of defining their clinical and biological significance. Among 373 children and adolescents (median age 8.8 years; range 1.9–16 years) analyzed using mRNA sequencing and/or multiplex RT-PCR, 29 patients were identified with kinase or cytokine receptor fusions involving CRLF2 (n=14), PDGFRB (n=8), ABL1 (n=3), JAK2 (n=2), EPOR (n=3), and LYN (n=1). There was only one fusion involving the LYN kinase gene, indicating LYN fusions as rare oncogenic drivers in pediatric B-ALL. The 5' partner for the LYN fusion was the NCOR1 gene, and the gene expression profile of the NCOR1::LYN positive case resembled BCR::ABL1–positive ALL, supporting its classification within the Ph-like ALL spectrum. The studied patients showed characteristic high-risk features, including male predominance, older age at diagnosis, high white blood cell counts, and enrichment for NCI high-risk disease, as well as a high frequency of IKZF1 deletions (~73%). Clinically, outcomes were poor with conventional therapy alone, with 5-year event-free and overall survival rates of 48.6% and 73.5%, respectively, and inferior survival compared with fusion-negative cases in the mRNA-seq cohort. The study supports that B-ALLs with fusions involving the LYN kinase gene are associated with the BCR::ABL1 like subtype of the disease.

In this 2022 study, the authors investigate the oncogenic role of the MYB::TYK2 fusion gene in high-risk B-lymphoblastic leukemia (HR B-ALL). TYK2 rearrangements are identified as recurrent events in the high-risk BCR::ABL1-like (Ph-like) ALL subtype. The study functionally characterizes the MYB::TYK2 fusion, which was initially isolated from a patient with this aggressive leukemia. Through in vitro and in vivo modeling, the authors demonstrate that the MYB::TYK2 fusion is a driver oncogene that confers cytokine-independent growth in vitro and leads to the development of B-ALL in mice . The authors propose that TYK2 fusions share similar breakpoints and likely lead to constitutive TYK activation by disrupting its auto-inhibitory domain. Importantly, the study shows that the MYB::TYK2 fusion constitutively activates the JAK/STAT signaling pathway in the studied model systems, consistent with its association with the BCR::ABL1-like (Ph-like) ALL subtype.

RET is a known oncogene that encodes a receptor tyrosine kinase with important roles in cell growth, differentiation, and survival. Germline M918T is strongly linked with multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B (MEN 2B) and its associated medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC). Somatic M918T is strongly associated with sporadic MTC. This study sought to elucidate the functional mechanisms and molecular properties of M918T RET protein. Isothermal titration calorimetry showed that M918T had >10-fold greater affinity for ATP compared to wildtype. Stoichiometry calculations and analytic gel filtration also suggest that M918T molecules are more likely to form dimers that associate with two ATP molecules compared to the single binding site for wild-type. In vitro kinase assays suggest that M918T increased stability of enzyme-ATP complex, strengthening ATP-binding, and achieving increased kinase activity at lower ATP concentrations compared to wildtype. Immunoprecipitation and western blotting experiments showed that M918T was more highly auto-phosphorylated in the presence or absence of ligand stimulation. Differential scanning calorimetry suggested that M918T may have changes in intramolecular interactions and reduced conformational rigidity that might play a significant role in M918T protein function. In low-stringency nonreducing conditions they show that M918T RET can dimerize and become autophosphorylated even in the absence of ligand stimulation. Taken together, these experiments and others suggest multiple distinct but complementary molecular mechanisms by which M918T leads to functional activation of RET relative to wild-type.

evidence.evidence_statement: In an open-label, multicenter, multicohort phase 1–2 study of non-small cell lung carcinoma (NCT05099172; total n = 209), single-agent sevabertinib 20 mg BID demonstrated clinically meaningful activity in ERBB2 (HER2)–mutant disease. This population predominantly involves HER2 tyrosine kinase domain (TKD) mutations (90–97% across cohorts), including exon 20 insertion - Y772_A775dupYVMA (60–79%). Confirmed ORR was 64% (95% CI 53 - 75; n = 81; CR 2%, PR 62%, SD 25%) in previously treated patients without prior HER2-targeted therapy, 38% (95% CI 25 - 52; n = 55; CR 5%, PR 33%, SD 42%) in patients previously treated with HER2-directed ADCs, and 71% (95% CI 59 - 81; n = 73; CR 4%, PR 67%, SD 22%) in treatment-naive locally advanced or metastatic disease. Corresponding mPFS 8.3 mo (95% CI 6.9 - 12.3), 5.5 mo (95% CI 4.3 - 8.3), and NE (95% CI 9.6 - NE), and mDoR 9.2 mo (95% CI 6.3 - 13.5), 8.5 mo (95% CI 5.6 - 16.4), and 11.0 mo (95% CI 8.1 -NE), respectively. Exploratory analyses showed higher response and longer PFS in HER2 TKD mutations vs non-TKD alterations (n = 73 vs 7), with ORR 70% (95% CI 58 - 80) vs 14% (95% CI <1 - 58) and mPFS 9.6 mo (95% CI 6.9 - 12.3) vs 6.9 mo (95% CI 2.5 - NE). In Y772_A775dupYVMA vs other HER2 TKD variants (n = 49 vs 23), with ORR 78% (95% CI 63 - 88) vs 57% (95% CI 35 - 77) and mPFS 12.2 mo (95% CI 6.9 - 16.4) vs 7.0 mo (95% CI 4.0 - NE). These findings support ERBB2 (HER2) mutation, particularly TKD exon 20 insertions, as predictive of response to sevabertinib.

Exploratory analyses showed higher response and longer PFS in HER2 TKD mutations vs non-TKD alterations (n = 73 vs 7), with ORR 70% (95% CI 58 - 80) vs 14% (95% CI <1 - 58) and mPFS 9.6 mo (95% CI 6.9 - 12.3) vs 6.9 mo (95% CI 2.5 - NE). In Y772_A775dupYVMA vs other HER2 TKD variants (n = 49 vs 23), with ORR 78% (95% CI 63 - 88) vs 57% (95% CI 35 - 77) and mPFS 12.2 mo (95% CI 6.9 - 16.4) vs 7.0 mo (95% CI 4.0 - NE). These findings support ERBB2 (HER2) mutation, particularly TKD exon 20 insertions, as predictive of response to sevabertinib.

This population predominantly involves HER2 tyrosine kinase domain (TKD) mutations (90–97% across cohorts), including exon 20 insertion - Y772_A775dupYVMA (60–79%). evidence.evidence_statement: In this 2020 case report, the authors present a pediatric patient with relapsed B-lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL), providing critical evidence for the diagnostic and therapeutic role of LYN fusions. The patient was a 6-year-old male who presented with high-risk features, including an initial white blood cell count of 883 × 10⁹/L and a relapsed disease that was refractory to re-induction chemotherapy. Comprehensive molecular diagnostics performed at relapse, including karyotyping and FISH, identified a balanced t(8;17)(q12;p11.2) translocation, which was subsequently confirmed by sequencing to generate an in-frame NCOR1::LYN fusion gene. This fusion joined exon 34 of NCOR1 to exon 8 of LYN, retaining the intact tyrosine kinase domain. Additional high-risk genetic lesions, including deletions of IKZF1 and CDKN2A, were also present. Upon identification of this ABL/SRC-family kinase fusion, the patient was treated with the tyrosine kinase inhibitor dasatinib (60 mg/m²/day) as monotherapy, achieving a complete morphologic and molecular remission within two weeks. This rapid response provided the first direct clinical evidence that leukemias driven by LYN fusions are exquisitely sensitive to dasatinib. The patient subsequently underwent haploidentical stem cell transplantation and remained in minimal residual disease-negative remission on dasatinib maintenance. The authors concluded that the NCOR1::LYN fusion is a recurrent, targetable oncogenic driver in high-risk pediatric B-ALL. Response of the described leukemia to treatment with a kinase inhibitor supports association of the NCOR1::LYN fusion with the Philadelphia chromosome-like (BCR::ABL1-like) subtype, in which activated kinase signaling is the defining molecular feature.

In this 2014 genomic profiling study of 1,725 patients with precursor B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL), the authors define the high-risk "Philadelphia chromosome-like" (Ph-like or BCR::ABL1-like) subgroup. This subgroup is characterized by a gene expression profile similar to BCR::ABL1-positive ALL, a high frequency of IKZF1 alterations, and a diverse spectrum of genetic alterations that constitutively activate kinase and cytokine receptor signaling pathways. The cohort included children, adolescents, and young adults up to age 39. RNA sequencing was performed on 136 patients with Ph-like ALL. The study identified kinase-activating alterations in 91% of Ph-like ALL cases. Among these, a novel MYB::TYK2 fusion was identified in one patient. The fusion retained an intact tyrosine kinase domain, and its identification classified this patient's leukemia within the "other JAK-STAT" activating alteration subgroup of Ph-like ALL. The authors concluded that Ph-like ALL is a common, high-risk subtype characterized by a range of genomic alterations activating a limited set of signaling pathways, nearly all of which are potentially amenable to inhibition with approved tyrosine kinase inhibitors. They propose that identifying these alterations, including rare fusions like MYB::TYK2, is critical for directing targeted therapy to improve patient outcomes.

In this 2023 study, the authors evaluated the diagnostic utility of NR4A3 immunohistochemistry in acinic cell carcinoma (AciCC) of the salivary gland. The cohort included 128 AciCCs, comprising 85 classic low-grade, 36 with high-grade transformation (HGT), and 7 high-grade tumors. NR4A3 rearrangements were assessed using a custom dual-color break-apart FISH probe. NR4A3 immunoreactivity was observed in 105 of 128 cases (82%), with similar positivity rates across low-grade, HGT, and high-grade AciCCs (82%, 81%, and 86%, respectively). FISH analysis was performed in 57 cases, confirming NR4A3 rearrangements in 23 of 28 (82%) low-grade cases, 11 of 14 (79%) HGT cases, and 2 of 2 (100%) high-grade cases, resulting in an overall confirmation rate of 36 of 44 (82%) in analyzable immunopositive tumors. Eight immunopositive cases (18%) were FISH-negative, while among 10 immunonegative cases, 2 of 8 analyzable tumors (25%) demonstrated NR4A3 rearrangement. Five cases were not evaluable by FISH. The authors conclude that NR4A3 rearrangements are strongly associated with AciCC and that NR4A3 immunohistochemistry is a robust and reliable tool for the differential diagnosis of this tumor.

The MYSTIC study compared response rates for immunotherapy verses chemotherapy. Specifically looking at the efficacy of the anti-PD-L1 therapy, durvalumab, with/without the anti-CTLA-4 therapy, tremelimumab, compared to platinum-based chemotherapy for overall survival (OS) and progress free survival (PFS). When considering implementation of immunotherapy (immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs)), there is a strong correlation between tumors that have high tumor mutational burden (TMB) and success of ICI. Tumor mutational burden can be calculated from both tumor sample (tTMB) and circulating tumor DNA that has been shed and is now collected in the blood (bTMB). This study showed that bTMB, which is less invasive and captures more of the tumor mutational heterogeneity, can be used for determining whether patients should use ICIs in the setting of metastatic NSCLC. From MYSTIC phase III trial, 1001 of the 1118 patients had adequate plasma samples available and of those, 809 samples had valid bTMB score (meaning above the variant allele frequency (VAF) needed for NGS assays; 809/1001 = 81%). Of those 809 patients, 735 of them had tumor samples available, however 275 samples did not meet criteria for “valid” tTMB due to insufficient tumor sample, insufficient DNA yield, or insufficient VAF to calculate TMB. Ultimately TMB scores from blood were more likely to be valid as compared to TMB scores from tumors. When comparing the shared mutations from matched tumor and blood sequencing assays, across a shared DNA region, 50% of mutations detected were found both in the blood and tumor samples. Furthermore, when matching the tumor and plasma samples, there was a positive correlation between the bTMB and tTMB. When comparing the discordance between bTMB and tTMB, multiple factors should be considered including assay-specific differences in genes tested and TMB algorithms, as well as sample differences, such as the intratumoral heterogeneity common in NSCLC. When considering bTMB scores in clinical outcomes, having greater than 20 mutations per megabase (mut/Mb) had the most favorable OS and PFS when treated with durvalumab plus tremelimumab compared to chemotherapy.

profile.name: TMB High
profile.summary: Tumors with a high mutational burden (TMB-High) are reported to have increased sensitivity to immunotherapy. High Tumor Mutation Burden is defined as 10 or more mutations per MB of DNA in an FDA approved companion diagnostic test based on next generation sequencing.

evidence.evidence_statement: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have been revolutionary in treating solid cancers, however the responses to these therapies can be quite variable. Though response rate to these immunotherapies is often correlated with tumor mutational burden (TMB), this might not be true across all cancer types. Within gastrointestinal tumors, the majority are microsatellite stable (MSS) which has mixed efficacy when treated with ICI compared to microsatellite instability-high (MSI-H) gastrointestinal tumors that respond well to ICIs. Previous studies were unsuccessful in showing a correlation between tumor mutational burden (TMB) status and MSS for predicting clinical response to ICI. This study found that the combination of TMB-H status with mutations in specific genes had increased response to ICIs, likely due to the quality of the neoantigens presented in these tumors. 48,606 samples with confirmed gastrointestinal cancer were binned into three groups 1) MSS-TMB-H (3.29%) 2) dMMR/MSI-H (4.67%) and 3) MSS-TMB-L (92.03%). These samples were sequenced using either NextSeq or NovaSeq, which used NGS for 592 or 700 genes respectively. Tumors were considered TMB-H if they had greater than or equal to 10 mutations per megabase (mut/Mb). Within the sequence analysis for the TMB-H/MSI-H groups, a subset of genes had a positive association with antitumor response, these genes are referred to as the modified TMB (mTMB) signature genes (CDC73, CTNNA1, ERBB4, EZH2, JAK2, MAP2K1, MAP2K4, PIK3R1, POLE, PPP2R1A, PPP2R2A, PTPN11, RAF1, RUNX1, STAG2 , and XPO1). Furthermore, within the MSS-TMB-H group, there was a significantly higher rate of amplification of CCND1 and FGF genes, most of which are located on 11q13. MSS tumors with a mutation in the mTMB genes had distinctive molecular profiles (high mutation counts, indels, SNVs) and immune response indicators (neoantigens and B-cell receptor richness, higher IFN gamma signatures, higher infiltration of NK cells, M1-like macrophages, and Th1 cells, but lower infiltration of M2-like macrophages). Patients with mTMB mutations treated with ICIs had longer overall survival compared to mTMB wildtype patients treated with ICIs within the CARIS and MSKCC cohorts. Importantly, for patients that did not receive ICIs, there was no difference between the OS and mTMB gene signature.

This study presented clinicopathological and molecular findings of TFCP2-rearranged rhabdomyosarcomas with epithelioid and/or spindle cell morphology. The cohort comprised 14 cases, including 3 index cases published in 2018. Six males and 8 females were included, with an age range of 11-86 years at diagnosis (mean: 31 years). Tumors were located in the bones (n=12/14) or soft tissue (n=2/14). TFCP2 gene fusions from FFPE materials were identified by RNA-seq (n=10/10) or anchored multiplex PCR (n=4/4), showing that exons 5 or 6 of FUS (n=8) or EWSR1 (n=6) were fused to exon 2 of TFCP2. FISH analyses were performed in select cases using EWSR1, FUS, and TFCP2 break-apart probes, showing positivity in 2 of 3, 5 of 5, and 9 of 9 tested cases, respectively. Homozygous deletion of CDKN2A was detected by aCGH in all tested cases (n=9/9), and mutations in the exon 1 of MYOD1 were absent (DNA, n=0/8; RNA, n=0/10) by Sanger sequencing. ALK overexpression was found in most cases (n=11/14) without underlying ALK fusion identified by either break-apart FISH (n=0/5) or NGS (n=0/14). Seven EWSR1/FUS::TFCP2 cases were subjected to unsupervised consensus clustering analyses, showing distinct segregation from the other rhabdomyosarcomas that include embryonal rhabdomyosarcomas (n=6), alveolar rhabdomyosarcomas (n=8), MYOD1-mutated rhabdomyosarcomas (n=4), and VGLL2-fused rhabdomyosarcomas (n=5). Collectively, this study showed that TFCP2-rearranged rhabdomyosarcomas exhibit recurrent EWSR1/FUS::TFCP2 gene fusions and are distinct from other rhabdomyosarcoma subtypes.

This study presented clinicopathological and molecular features of 11 cases of head and neck rhabdomyosarcomas (HNRMSs). The median age of the cohort was 29 years, ranging 16-74 years with no sex bias. All cases but one were intraosseous, involving the mandible (n=4), maxilla (n=3), and skull (n=3). The remaining case occurred in the superficial cervical soft tissue. Molecularly, FUS::TFCP2 (n=7) and EWSR1::TFCP2 (n=4) gene fusions were identified by FISH analyses and/or targeted DNA/RNA sequencing. ALK expression was detected in most cases by IHC (n=9/10), with an intragenic deletion identified in 43% of tested cases (n=3/7). CDKN2A loss was identified in all 5 tested cases. The lesions displayed characteristic spindle and epithelioid morphology. The authors also performed a literature review and included 27 TFCP2-rearranged HNRMS cases, showing that this disease mostly affects young adults and pediatric patients. In summary, HNRMSs with spindle cell and epitheloid phenotype exhibit recurrent EWSR1/FUS::TFCP2 gene fusions and preferentially arise in the skeleton.

This study reported clinicopathologic and molecular features of 25 cases of fusion-driven spindle cell/sclerosing rhabdomyosarcoma (SCSRMS). The tumors occurred in bone (n=19) and soft tissue (n=6). The bone tumor cohort included 6 male and 13 female patients, with an age range of 13-74 years (median age: 41 years), whereas the soft tissue tumors occurred in 4 men and 2 women, with an age range of 28-71 years (median age: 50 years ). In bone tumor cases, 17 of 19 cases were analyzed by NGS with the remaining 2 cases only studied by FISH. NGS analyses revealed the following gene fusions: FUS::TFCP2 (n=12/17), EWSR1::TFCP2 (n=3/17), and MEIS1::NCOA2 (n=2/17), with exon breakpoints identified. Specifically, exon 5 of EWSR1 was joined to exon 2 of TFCP2 in all 3 EWSR1::TFCP2 cases. FISH also successfully identified EWSR1 rearrangements (n=2/2). Among the studied soft tissue tumor cases 1 of 6 showed exon 5 of EWSR1 fused to exon 2 of TFCP2 by NGS, whereas the remaining 5 cases exhibited non-TFCP2 gene fusions. The study confirms EWSR1::TFCP2 as one of the primary oncogenic drivers in bone and soft tissue SCSRMS.

In this 2019 study, the authors aimed to evaluate the usefulness of NR4A3 immunostaining and compare it with NR4A3 Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) for the differential diagnosis of acinic cell carcinoma (AciCC). The study included 64 AciCC cases (53 low-grade tumors and 11 with high-grade transformation), 29 mammary analogue secretory carcinoma (MASC), and 70 other salivary gland carcinomas, evaluated by NR4A3 immunostaining. NR4A3 immunostaining was considered positive when moderate to strong nuclear staining was observed, while cytoplasmic staining was regarded as nonspecific. Moderate to strong nuclear NR4A3 expression was detected in 63 of 64 AciCCs (98%), including all high-grade transformed cases; only one case was negative. In contrast, none of the MASCs or other salivary gland carcinomas showed nuclear NR4A3 staining. These findings confirmed specific association of the NR4A3 rearrangement and upregulation with AciCC. FISH analysis was successfully performed in 58 AciCCs, of which 49 cases (84%) showed abnormal NR4A3 signals consistent with gene translocation (44 with split signals and 5 with single red signals). Nine cases (16%) showed normal FISH results. Samples were classified as positive when more than 20% of 50 counted nuclei displayed abnormal signals. The authors concluded that NR4A3 rearrangement is highly associated with AciCC and the immunostaining is sensitive and specific marker for AciCC, including high-grade cases. The studies shows utility of confirming NR4A3 rearrangement by immunostaining and FISH in distinguishing AciCC from MASC.

In this 2018 study by Keiko Segawa et al., the authors analyzed 22 tumors, including 16 clear cell sarcomas of soft tissue (CCSST) and 6 clear cell sarcoma–like gastrointestinal tumors (CCSLGT), to characterize EWSR1-related gene rearrangements using FISH and RT-PCR. EWSR1 rearrangement was identified in 93.8% (15/16) of CCSSTs and 66.7% (4/6) of CCSLGTs. In CCSST, 68.8% of cases showed concurrent ATF1 rearrangement, supporting the presence of the EWSR1::ATF1 fusion as the predominant genetic alteration; this was confirmed by RT-PCR in tested cases. In contrast, CCSLGT demonstrated a more heterogeneous fusion pattern, with both EWSR1::ATF1 and EWSR1::CREB1 detected (each in 33.3% of cases). Rare CREM rearrangements were also observed in both tumor types. Overall, the study reinforces the strong association of EWSR1::ATF1 fusion with clear cell sarcoma of soft tissue, while EWSR1::CREB1 appears relatively more frequent in gastrointestinal counterparts, highlighting the diagnostic utility of identifying specific EWSR1 fusion partners in distinguishing these related entities.

In this 2002 study by Cristina R Antonescu et al., 12 histologically confirmed cases of clear cell sarcoma (CCS) arising in the deep soft tissues of the extremities were analyzed to assess the prevalence and diagnostic utility of the EWSR1::ATF1 fusion using RT-PCR on both frozen and formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tissue. Histologically, 10 of 12 cases exhibited the classic nested epithelioid morphology with clear to pale eosinophilic cytoplasm, central nuclei, and prominent nucleoli. Immunohistochemistry showed diffuse positivity for HMB45 and MITF in all cases, and S-100 in 10 cases, supporting melanocytic differentiation. Ultrastructural analysis revealed melanosomes in 6 of 7 examined tumors. Molecular analysis detected the EWSR1::ATF1 fusion transcript in 11 of 12 cases (91%), all demonstrating the in-frame fusion of EWSR1 exon 8 to ATF1 codon 65, with no variant structures identified. RT-PCR for MITF transcripts confirmed expression of the melanocyte-specific MITF-M isoform in all tested cases. These findings establish EWSR1::ATF1 as a highly sensitive and recurrent molecular marker for CCS. Its detection serves as a reliable diagnostic tool, differentiating CCS from morphologic mimics such as malignant melanoma, and confirms CCS as a genetically defined, melanocytic sarcoma driven by this characteristic fusion.

The PAX5::AUTS2 fusion represents a rare but clinically significant genetic subtype of childhood and young-adolescent B-cell precursor acute lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL). An international cohort of 50 patients—including 16 previously reported cases—was assembled, with fusion status confirmed or predicted through a combination of conventional karyotyping, fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH), SNP array analysis, optical genome mapping (OGM), RT PCR, whole genome sequencing, and whole exome sequencing. Cohort analyses consistently demonstrate that PAX5::AUTS2 is associated with high relapse rates, frequent central nervous system involvement, and poor event-free and overall survival, with particularly adverse outcomes observed in very young children. The study reported a 5-year cumulative incidence of relapse of approximately 48% and an event-free survival of roughly 48%, highlighting a prognosis inferior to most standard-risk B ALL groups. Infants and toddlers (<3 years) comprise the majority of cases and are most vulnerable. Collectively, these findings support the classification of PAX5::AUTS2 B ALL as a high-risk subtype requiring intensified frontline therapy and enhanced CNS-directed management. evidence.evidence_statement: This retrospective analysis of the Phase 3 EAGLE trial (NCT02369874) evaluated tissue tumor mutational burden (tTMB) and blood TMB (bTMB) as predictive biomarkers in platinum-refractory recurrent or metastatic head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC). Using WES, tTMB (n=153) was calculated from somatic SNVs and indels (<20,bp) at 5–80% allele frequency. bTMB (n=247) was determined using the GuardantOMNI assay (500 genes; 2,Mb), incorporating variants across all allele frequencies. In the tissue-evaluable cohort, cutoffs from 10 to 20 mut/Mb were assessed. For durvalumab monotherapy, a 10 mut/Mb threshold showed the best discrimination [HR: 0.72 (CI: 0.45–1.15)], though OS differences were not significant. For durvalumab plus tremelimumab, significant OS benefit was observed at 10 [HR: 0.52 (CI: 0.28–0.98)] and 12 mut/Mb [HR: 0.46 (CI: 0.24–0.86)] cutoffs. At 10 mut/Mb, median OS for high- vs. low-tTMB was 9.9 vs. 4.4 months (durvalumab) and 16.0 vs. 3.3 months (combination). In the blood-evaluable cohort, bTMB ≥ 16mut/Mb was the optimal predictive threshold. Patients with bTMB ≥ 16 achieved superior survival over chemotherapy for both durvalumab (OS HR: 0.39; PFS HR: 0.48) and combination therapy (OS HR: 0.38; PFS HR: 0.45). Median OS for bTMB ≥ 16 was 8.1 (durvalumab) and 7.6 (combination) vs. 4.0 months (SoC); benefits were absent in patients with bTMB < 16. These findings suggest tTMB ≥ 10 and bTMB ≥16 mut/Mb as robust predictive thresholds for identifying HNSCC patients benefiting from checkpoint inhibition.

evidence.evidence_statement: This analysis of the Phase 2 KEYNOTE-782 trial (NCT03664024) evaluated the correlation of blood tumor mutational burden (bTMB) with the efficacy of first-line pembrolizumab plus platinum-based chemotherapy in patients with metastatic non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). The cfDNA assay utilized was GRAIL, comprising 654 genes (1.9 Mb). Paired white blood cells were sequenced to eliminate mutations related to clonal hematopoiesis and germline variants. bTMB was calculated as the total number of nonsynonymous mutations per megabase pair of the sequenced genome. In the bTMB-evaluable population (n=101), the distribution of bTMB scores was found to be similar among both responders and non-responders. Consequently, the study concluded that bTMB does not have predictive value for the efficacy of pembrolizumab combined with platinum-based chemotherapy in this clinical setting.

evidence.evidence_statement: In this study, the authors analyzed 14 cases of angiomatoid fibrous histiocytoma (AFH). The EWSR1::CREB1 fusion associated with t(2;22)(q33;q12) was detected in 13 of 14 tumors by dual‑color and four‑color FISH, demonstrating rearrangement of the EWSR1 and CREB1 loci. In the case with available frozen tissue, RT‑PCR confirmed an in‑frame EWSR1::CREB1 transcript. Sequencing studies indicate that the fusion typically joins the EWSR1 N‑terminal activation domain (commonly exon 7) to the CREB1 bZIP DNA‑binding region (commonly exon 7), generating an intact chimeric transcription factor that drives aberrant CREB‑mediated transcription. Although exon‑specific breakpoints were not detailed in this study, the RT‑PCR–verified transcript is consistent with the canonical EWSR1‑exon‑7::CREB1‑exon‑7 configuration described in AFH. These findings establish EWSR1::CREB1 as a highly specific diagnostic biomarker that helps distinguish AFH from clear cell sarcoma and other histologic mimics with alternative EWSR1 fusion partners.

In this study, the authors report a 34‑year-old patient with angiomatoid fibrous histiocytoma (AFH) who initially presented with a pulmonary nodule and a 4th‑rib lesion and subsequently developed metastases to the iliac bone, subcutaneous tissue, pleura, lymph nodes, and brain. FISH confirmed an EWSR1::CREB1 rearrangement, and RNA-based next-generation sequencing identified an in-frame EWSR1 exon 7–CREB1 exon 7 fusion. This molecular finding established the AFH diagnosis across multiple lesions despite the tumor’s atypical and highly metastatic presentation. The disease progressed systemically, resulting in death 18 months after initial surgery, representing the first documented case of fatal, multi-organ metastatic EWSR1::CREB1–positive AFH and highlighting the rare but significant potential for aggressive behavior in tumors harboring this fusion.

In this study, the authors analyzed 9 cases of angiomatoid fibrous histiocytoma (AFH). The EWSR1::CREB1 fusion was identified as the predominant molecular alteration, detected in 8 of 9 tumors by RT‑PCR and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, which demonstrated an identical junction of EWSR1 exon 7 fused to CREB1 exon 7 in all positive cases. FISH analysis showed EWSR1 rearrangement in 7 of 8 evaluable tumors, and conventional cytogenetic analysis in one case revealed a t(2;22)(q33;q12) translocation. These complementary molecular techniques establish EWSR1::CREB1 as the most frequent and characteristic fusion in AFH, serving as a highly useful diagnostic marker that distinguishes AFH from other round/spindle cell sarcomas, including Ewing sarcoma and clear cell sarcoma.

This landmark study provided revised classification of B-lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL) based on integrated genomic findings from 1,988 childhood and adult B-ALLs. All cases were subjected to RNA-seq analysis, and a subset of them were further characterized by WGS (n=17), WES (n=73), and SNP array (n=1,141). Among 23 described subtypes, two were related to the alterations of B-lineage transcription factor gene PAX5 despite showing different gene expression patterns, and were designated as PAX5alt and PAX5 p.P80R groups. The first group included diverse PAX5 alterations, including gene fusions, non-p.P80R mutations, and/or intrachromosomal focal amplification (PAX5amp). PAX5 fusions were found in 57 cases (38.5% of the PAXalt group); they were in-frame and involved 24 partner genes, the most frequent of which were ETV6 (n=19), NOL4L (n=5), AUTS2 (n=4), and CBFA2T3 (n=4). Importantly, PAX5::JAK2 were observed exclusively in Ph-like B-ALL, and PAX5::ZCCHC7 were observed in B-ALL cases with other subtype-specific pathognomonic events. In summary, PAX5 fusions, except PAX5::JAK2 and PAX5::ZCCHC7, are subtype-defining alterations for the PAX5alt B-ALL.

This European population-based cohort study examined the genomic landscape of 110 consecutively diagnosed childhood (aged 1-18 years) “B-other” lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) cases, collected over 7 years in the Czech Republic. The B-other ALL was defined as B-ALL negative for ETV6::RUNX1, BCR::ABL1, TCF3::PBX1, KMT2A-rearrangements, hyperdiploidy (>50 chromosomes), and hypodiploidy (<44 chromosomes). Molecular alterations were characterized using a combination of SNP arrays (n=103), WES (n=109), and RNA-seq (n=69) as well as RT-PCR and flow cytometry for select alterations. In-frame PAX5 gene fusions were identified in 14 patients, involving 11 distinct fusion partners. Of those, ten fusion types retained a large 5’ portion of PAX5 (exons 1-5/6/7/8) joined to partner genes. The remaining PAX5::ZCCHC7 fusion (n=2 cases), generated by an intrachromosomal inversion joining PAX5 with its adjacent gene ZCCHC7, resulted in near-complete loss of PAX5. This finding suggests distinct biological characteristics of PAX5::ZCCHC7 in B-ALL leukemogenesis compared to other PAX5 fusions. In summary, PAX5 fusions, except PAX5::ZCCHC7, represent primary oncogenic drivers in 11% (12/110) of B-other ALL.

This large FISH-based screening study systematically identified PAX5 fusion partners in a cohort of 446 patients with childhood acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL). Interphase FISH was performed on all cases and revealed patterns suggestive of PAX5 rearrangements in 10 cases, corresponding to 2.2% of tested childhood ALLs and 2.6% of B-cell ALLs. Using a combination of RACE (rapid amplification of cDNA ends) with Sanger sequencing and fusion gene-specific RT-PCR, the authors identified PAX5 fusion partners in 9 of 10 cases. In addition to the previously reported PAX5 partners (PML, ETV6, and H20orf112), this study identified five novel gene partners, including transcription regulators (HIPK1 and DACH1), scaffold proteins (POM121C, BRD1), and a kinase (JAK2). The study showed that PAX5 fusions represent important class of primary oncogenic alterations in B-ALL.

In this 2020 study, the authors analyzed clinical, histopathologic, and RNA sequencing data from 37 infants with rhabdomyosarcoma (RMS) diagnosed before six months of age. The median age of the cohort was 2.8 months (range 0–5.8 months). Spindle cell RMS (SRMS) was identified in eight (22%) patients. Among these, VGLL2 fusions were detected in three cases, with NCOA2 (n = 2) or CITED2 (n = 1) as fusion partners. Histologically, these VGLL2-positive tumors displayed a fibromatous-like spindle cell pattern. Fusion-positive SRMS cases were associated with favorable outcomes and long-term survival. Overall, the authors highlighted VGLL2 fusions as a diagnostic biomarker for infantile SRMS, enabling molecular distinction from embryonal and alveolar RMS subtypes.

In this 2021 study, the authors analyzed clinical, pathologic, molecular, and radiologic features of 4 pediatric patients with VGLL2-rearranged infantile sclerosing and spindle-cell rhabdomyosarcoma (ssRMS). Three patients were diagnosed at birth and one at 12 months of age. All primary tumors were localized but considered unresectable, and initial management included chemotherapy or observation. RNA sequencing confirmed VGLL2::NCOA2 or VGLL2::CITED2 fusion transcripts in all cases. Three patients showed high-grade sarcomatous transformation at progression, whereas one retained low-grade morphology in a metastatic adrenal lesion. Metastatic spread occurred in 3 patients (lungs, bone, lymph nodes, adrenal), and 2 patients died of disease. Whole-exome sequencing revealed low mutational burden in primary tumors and increased genomic instability with patient-specific alterations at relapse, including TP53, CDKN2A/B, and FGFR4 mutations. Transcriptomic clustering confirmed that both low- and high-grade tumors retained VGLL2-rearranged RMS signatures. The study highlights that VGLL2-rearranged RMS, although often described as indolent, can progress aggressively, especially when initial surgical resection is not feasible.

In this 2020 study, the authors analyzed four cases of follicular lymphoma using circulating tumor DNA and droplet digital PCR to monitor EZH2 hotspot mutations, including A682G. One patient with transformed follicular lymphoma carried the EZH2 A682G mutation with a variant allele frequency of 1.8% in a bone marrow biopsy; seven months later, after multiple failed lines of therapy, the mutation was detected concurrently at 38.2% in a lymph node biopsy and 74.0% in circulating tumor DNA shortly before the patient's death. In this patient, the A682G mutation persisted across multiple anatomical sites and coincided with immunochemotherapy resistance, aggressive transformation, and a fatal disease outcome. Furthermore, the patient's EZH2 mutation levels in circulating tumor DNA tracked with tumor burden and PET-CT findings, suggesting that monitoring the persistent A682G mutation may reflect disease progression and treatment failure. The authors note that activating EZH2 mutations, including A682G, are clinically relevant in follicular lymphoma (occurring in ~25% of patients) and suggest they can serve as biomarkers for tumor burden and disease aggressiveness, supporting an oncogenic association of EZH2 A682G in follicular lymphoma.

In this 2013 study, the authors analyzed 366 follicular lymphoma (FL) patients with additional paired samples from 33 cases of transformed FL. Patients harbored EZH2 mutations predominantly at codons Y646, A682, and A692, with variant allele frequencies (VAFs) ranging from 2% to 61%. In total, 9 A682G mutations were detected. Comparative analysis with other recurrently mutated genes (CREBBP, MLL2, TNFRSF14, and MEF2B) demonstrated that the majority of EZH2 mutations were clonal. Gene expression analysis of high tumor-content samples identified 106 differentially expressed genes associated with EZH2-mutant cases. The authors conclude that EZH2 mutations act as early events in follicular lymphoma and contribute to disease pathogenesis.

This is part of a randomised phase 3 trial, CheckpOiNt Blockade For the Inihibition of Relapsed Mesothelioma (CONFIRM), that examined therapeutic response to the anti-PD1 inhibitor, nivolumab, in patients with relapsed mesothelioma. Patients were randomised to receive nivolumab (221 patients, 6 cycles without dose reduction) or placebo (111 patients, 4 cycles). As part of the exploratory multi-omic analysis, tumour mutational burden (TMB) was measured via whole transcriptome sequencing on the archival formalin fixed tumour blocks of a subset of patients who achieved a partial response (R group, n = 12) or no response (NR group, n = 9) to nivolumab. No significant difference in TMB was observed between these two groups of patients (both approximately 5 mutations/ Mb).

This is part of the randomised double-blind phase 3 trial, CameL-sq, a study that assessed the therapeutic effectiveness of the PD-1 blockade, camrelizumab plus chemotherapy as first-line treatment in advanced lung squamous cell carcinoma (LUSC) patients. 389 treatment naïve state IIIB-IV LUSC patients negative of sensitising EGFR or ALK genetic alterations were randomised 1:1 to receive either camrelizumab (200mg) or placebo in combination with chemotherapy (5 mg/mL*min carboplatin and 175 mg/m2 paclitaxel). Part of this study explores the value of blood TMB (bTMB) as a predictive biomarker in this setting. For this analysis, baseline tissue and peripheral blood samples were collected prior to initial treatment and an on-treatment peripheral blood sample collected after two cycles of treatment for 270 patients (134 from the combination group, 136 from the chemo only group). Pre-treatment tissue TMB (tTMB), bTMB, and on-treatment bTMB were measured using next-generation sequencing on a pre-designed 543-gene panel. TMB was calculated as the number of nonsynonymous mutations (SNVs and InDels) in coding regions that met a certain sequencing depth (100x for tissue and 500x for plasma) and an allele frequency (5% for tissue and 0.7% for plasma) per Mg of the exonic region. Driver gene mutations and hotspot mutations included in the dbSNP138/COSMIC database were removed from the TMB calculation. The tTMB or bTMB-High groups were defined as those with a TMB value ≥ 75% level. Among patients that received the combination treatment, pre-treatment tTMB or bTMB showed no predictive or prognostic value. Conversely, on-treatment bTMB and the bTMB dynamics, measured by ∆bTMB (the difference between on-treatment and pretreatment bTMB levels), showed complementary and non-redundant predictive value for the therapeutic benefit of the combination treatment. Specifically, patients with low on-treatment bTMB achieved longer PFS (median PFS, 9.1 vs 4.1 months; HR = 0.190, P < 0.001) and OS (median, not reached vs 8.0 months; HR = 0.144, P < 0.001). Patients with increased or unchanged bTMB compared to pretreatment (∆bTMB ≥ 0) had shorter PFS (median, 4.5 vs 8.5 months; HR = 2.545, P < 0.001) and OS (median, 9.0 months vs not reached; HR = 4.199, P = 0.201) compared to those with reduced bTMB following treatment (∆bTMB < 0). Patients with low on-treatment bTMB and ∆bTMB < 0 had the longest PFS and OS, while those with high on-treatment bTMB and ∆bTMB ≥ 0 the worst PFS and OS. Notably, on-treatment bTMB predicts long-term benefit from camrelizumab plus chemotherapy among patients achieving initial radiologic stable disease. Among the 48 patients with initial SD from the combination treatment, those with high on-treatment bTMB had significantly poorer PFS (median, 4.1 vs 5.6 months; HR = 2.861, P = 0.002) and OS (median, 7.8 vs 18.2 months; HR = 3.546, P = 0.001) compared to patients with low on-treatment bTMB. In conclusion, the combination of on-treatment bTMB and its dynamics is predictive for the therapeutic benefit of camrelizumab in combination with chemotherapy in advanced LUSC patients.

The authors performed retrospective analysis of 66 myoepithelial (ME) tumors arising outside the salivary glands, including soft tissue, bone, and visceral lesions. The cohort included 36 females and 30 males, with a wide age range of 1 to 75 years (median 26 years). EWSR1 gene rearrangement was detected by fluorescence in situ hybridization in 30 (45%) cases. More than half of the cases (n=16) occurred in children and young adults (less than 30 years of age). Among cases positive for EWSR1 rearrangement, POU5F1 rearrangement was identified by FISH in 5 tumors (8%), all arising in the deep soft tissues of the extremities, typically showing a clear cell, nested morphology. An PBX1 rearrangement was found in 5 EWSR1 positive tumors, occurring in deep soft tissue, bone, and lung, often displaying bland spindle cell or clear epithelioid morphology. A single ZNF444 rearrangement was observed in an EWSR1 positive tumor occurring in a 64-year-old female in the lung. Tumors without identified fusion partners but harboring EWSR1 rearrangements (n=19) exhibited variable morphologies, including small blue cell, epithelioid, and spindle patterns. EWSR1-negative tumors (n=36, 55%) were more often benign, superficially located, or cutaneous, and sometimes showed ductal or glandular differentiation. Overall, the authors concluded that EWSR1 rearrangement is a common molecular event in ME tumors in soft tissues and is absent in myoepithelial carcinomas of the salivary gland and other related tumors.

In this 2024 study, the authors analyzed 40 myoepithelial tumors of soft tissue and bone arising in patients ≤21 years of age. The cohort included 22 females and 18 males, with ages ranging from 3 months to 21 years (median 11.5 years). Molecular testing demonstrated evidence of gene fusions in 9 of 21 (43%) tested cases. Rearrangements involving the EWSR1 gene were detected by FISH in 6 of 18 (33%) cases. Among cases analyzed by next-generation sequencing, an EWSR1::POU5F1 fusion was identified in one tumor, while additional non-EWSR1 fusions included FUS::KLF17 and BRD4::CITED1. Tumors harboring EWSR1 rearrangements did not show a single uniform morphology but were seen across both benign and malignant lesions with variable histologic patterns, including epithelioid, spindle, and mixed cell types in myxoid or chondroid backgrounds. EWSR1-negative tumors comprised a substantial proportion of cases and included tumors lacking both EWSR1 and FUS rearrangements, highlighting genetic heterogeneity in this entity. Overall, the authors concluded that while EWSR1 rearrangement represents a recurrent and diagnostically useful molecular alteration in a subset of pediatric myoepithelial tumors, it is not universally present, and its absence does not exclude the diagnosis. Therefore, integration of morphology, immunohistochemistry, and molecular testing is required for accurate diagnosis, with EWSR1 fusions serving as supportive but not definitive diagnostic markers.

In this 2011 study the authors analyzed 18 cutaneous myoepithelial tumors arising in 7 female and 11 male patients, with a median age of 56 years (range 34–86 years). Tumors included 9 mixed tumors, 8 myoepitheliomas, and 1 myoepithelial carcinoma. Tumor size ranged from 0.3 to 1.7 cm (mean 1.0 cm). Mixed tumors were mostly located on the head (n=8), while myoepitheliomas arose mainly in the extremities (n=6). One myoepithelial carcinoma occurred on the cheek. Histologically, mixed tumors displayed ductal structures with epithelioid, spindle, and plasmacytoid myoepithelial cells, whereas the myoepithelial carcinoma exhibited infiltrative atypical spindle cells with pleomorphic nuclei and 5 mitoses per 10 HPF. Immunohistochemistry showed universal positivity for EMA and calponin, with variable expression of S100 (90%), cytokeratin (80%), ASMA (78%), and GFAP (50%). By FISH analysis, 7 of 16 cases (44%) exhibited EWSR1 rearrangement: 4 mixed tumors, 2 myoepitheliomas, and 1 myoepithelial carcinoma. The identification of EWSR1 rearrangements across different histologic subtypes further supports a shared molecular pathogenesis. No FUS rearrangements were detected. Follow-up data, available for 5 patients including the carcinoma case, showed no evidence of disease over 6–72 months. Overall, the authors concluded that cutaneous myoepithelial tumors form a spectrum from benign mixed tumor to myoepithelioma and myoepithelial carcinoma and that a subset harbors EWSR1 rearrangements, linking them genetically to their soft tissue, bone, and visceral counterparts.

In this report the authors described a 9-year-old boy with a myoepithelioma arising in the right posterior mediastinum. The tumor’s deep location is exceptionally rare, with only four well-documented cases reported in the literature. Histologically, the tumor exhibited features consistent with myoepithelioma, and molecular testing using next-generation sequencing revealed an EWSR1::ZNF444 fusion involving exon 7 of EWSR1 and exon 5 of ZNF444. EWSR1 fusions are a common molecular feature in soft tissue myoepitheliomas and have been reported with diverse fusion partners including PBX1, ZNF444, POU5F1, ATF1, and PBX3. Other rare alterations such as PLAG1, FUS, SRF, OGT fusions, and SMARCB1/INI1 deficiency are more frequently observed in malignant cases. This case underscores the importance of integrating histopathology with molecular genetics, particularly EWSR1 fusion status, to ensure accurate diagnosis and inform prognostic assessment.

A 53-year-old Chinese man, a lifelong non-smoker, presented with chest tightness and pain. CT imaging revealed multiple small nodules in the right lower lobe of the lung. A biopsy confirmed stage IV lung adenocarcinoma with an EGFR exon 19 deletion. First-line treatment with Erlotinib (150 mg daily) resulted in a partial response, with regression of the tumors. After 28 months, disease progression was observed, characterized by enlargement of the primary tumor and the development of new bone metastases. Repeat biopsy confirmed the persistence of the EGFR exon 19 deletion along with the acquisition of a T790M mutation. The patient was subsequently treated with second-line Osimertinib (80 mg daily), achieving another partial response that lasted 15.4 months.

evidence.evidence_statement: Lorlatinib is an orally available, small molecule multi-targeted kinase inhibitor that is FDA-approved for the treatment of patients with ALK-positive metastatic non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) whose disease has progressed on crizotinib and at least one other ALK inhibitor for metastatic disease, alectinib as the first ALK inhibitor therapy for metastatic disease or ceritinib as the first ALK inhibitor therapy for metastatic disease. The NCCN Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer Guidelines (V5.2024) lists lorlatinib for the treatment of patients with ALK-positive NSCLC with ALK G1202R or ALK L1196M, excluding tumors harboring both ALK G1202R and L1196M as compound mutations. In the Phase II study of lorlatinib in patients with ALK-positive NSCLC harboring ALK resistance mutations, patients harboring ALK G1202R/del (n=27, ALK G1202R; n=1, ALK G1202del) demonstrated an overall response rate of 57% (95% CI=37-76), a median duration of response of seven months (95% CI=6.1-NR) and a median progression-free survival of 8.2 months (95% CI=5.6-25.6) (PMID: 30892989).

profile.name: ALK G1202R AND v::ALK Fusion
profile.summary: ALK fusion with G1202R mutation in the ALK kinase domain was first identified in a lung adenocarcinoma patient who had progressed after 10 months of responding to crizotinib. Further characterization of this variant verified crizotinib resistance and additionally demonstrated resistance to multiple next generation ALK inhibitors including ceritinib, alectinib and brigatinib. Experiments using the HSP90 inhibitor 17-AAG have indicated potential sensitivity of EML4-ALK G1202R to this drug, suggesting this variant may be an HSP90 client protein.

drug.mechanism: Multi-targeted kinase inhibitor (targets include ALK and ROS1 among others)

evidence.evidence_statement: Neladalkib is an orally available, small molecule ALK inhibitor. There are promising clinical data of response to neladalkib in patients with ALK G1202R-mutated non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). In the Phase I/II ALKOVE-1 (NCT05384626) trial of neladalkib in 32 patients with ALK-rearranged NSCLC harboring ALK G1202R single or compound mutations, the overall response rate (ORR) was 69% (22/32) (Abstract: Drilon, A. et al., Abstract# 1253O, ESMO 2024. https://www.annalsofoncology.org/article/S0923-7534(24)02829-1/fulltext). Of patients that were previously treated with lorlatinib (n=30) or were lorlatinib-naïve (n=2), the ORR was 67% (20/30) and 100% (2/2), respectively (Abstract: Drilon, A. et al., Abstract# 1253O, ESMO 2024. https://www.annalsofoncology.org/article/S0923-7534(24)02829-1/fulltext). In vivo studies with ALK-fusion positive xenograft models expressing ALK resistance mutations (ALK G1202R, G1202R/L1196M, G1202R/G1269A and G1202R/L1198F) demonstrated sensitivity to neladalkib as measured by reduced tumor size and prolonged survival (PMID: 39269178).

evidence.evidence_statement: Alectinib is a second-generation small molecule inhibitor of ALK. Across various studies, patients with ALK fusion-positive non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) have acquired ALK G1202R mutations upon disease progression with alectinib treatment (PMID: 29373100, 29376144, 24736079, 27432227, 27130468). In a longitudinal study of 22 ALK-positive patients with NSCLC who progressed on ALK tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs), five patients had ALK G1202R mutations upon disease progression with alectinib (PMID: 29376144). A separate study of resistance to ALK TKIs identified five patients with ALK-positive NSCLC who had a G1202R mutation upon progression with alectinib (PMID: 27432227). Additionally, case reports of resistance to second-generation ALK TKIs revealed G1202R as a mechanism of resistance to alectinib in two other patients (PMID: 24736079, 27130468). In vitro studies have demonstrated that alectinib fails to inhibit G1202R-mutant ALK at a clinically-achievable IC50 (PMID: 29650534).

evidence.evidence_statement: Brigatinib is an orally available, small molecule ALK inhibitor that is FDA-approved for the treatment of adult patients with ALK-positive metastatic non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), as detected by an FDA-approved test. ALK-rearrangements for treatment with brigatinib were detected by the Vysis ALK Break Apart FISH Probe Kit. ALK G1202R has been identified as an acquired resistance mutation in patients with ALK-positive NSCLC upon disease progression with brigatinib treatment. In a retrospective clinical study, three patients with ALK-positive NSCLC were treated with brigatinib and acquired ALK G1202R upon disease progression (PMID: 31358542). In a multicenter study, one patient with ALK-positive NSCLC and one patient with ALK-positive NSCLC with ALK V1180L were treated with brigatinib and acquired ALK G1202R upon disease progression, with one patient additionally acquiring ALK L1196M (PMID: 29935304). In a clinical study, three patients with ALK-positive lung adenocarcinoma were treated with brigatinib and acquired ALK G1202R upon disease progression (PMID: 27432227). Preclinical studies of ALK G1202R expressed in ALK-positive Ba/F3 cells demonstrate resistance to brigatinib as measured by increased IC50 values compared to wildtype (PMID: 27432227).
